lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding cholinesterase inhibitor therapy?

options.text: Commence donepezil as the presentation and imaging support behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not effective in behavioural-variant FTD and can worsen behavioural symptoms; the PBS listing for donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine applies to mild to moderate Alzheimer's dementia, not FTD (Source: PBS Anti-dementia listing; RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

options.text: Do not commence cholinesterase inhibitors as the picture supports behavioural-variant FTD
options.rationale: Behavioural-variant FTD (disinhibition, apathy, hyperorality, loss of empathy with preserved short-term memory and frontotemporal atrophy on imaging) does not respond to cholinesterase inhibitors and the PBS listing excludes this indication; management is behavioural and supportive with SSRI trials for specific target symptoms if needed (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia; PBS Anti-dementia listing).

options.text: Commence memantine as the first-line agent because it is licensed for all types of dementia
options.rationale: Memantine is PBS-listed for moderate to severe Alzheimer's dementia only and does not have an evidence base or listing in FTD (Source: PBS Anti-dementia listing).

options.text: Refer directly to neurosurgery for consideration of decompressive surgery
options.rationale: There is no neurosurgical indication in neurodegenerative frontotemporal atrophy; imaging shows atrophy, not a space-occupying process (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

options.text: Commence risperidone for the behavioural changes without further assessment
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are reserved for risk-of-harm situations in dementia and are not the first-line management of FTD behavioural change; SSRIs have a better evidence base for specific target symptoms and non-pharmacological measures come first (Source: RANZCP CPG: Dementia).

explanation.summary: Behavioural-variant FTD presents in the 50s to 60s with disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, hyperorality and stereotyped behaviours, with preserved short-term memory and frontotemporal atrophy on MRI. Unlike Alzheimer's, cholinesterase inhibitors are ineffective and can worsen behaviour; the AU PBS listing for cholinesterase inhibitors covers mild to moderate Alzheimer's dementia specifically. Management is behavioural and supportive; SSRIs may help specific target symptoms.
key_points: bvFTD: disinhibition, apathy, hyperorality, preserved memory
Cholinesterase inhibitors: PBS-listed for mild to moderate AD only
Memantine: moderate to severe AD only
SSRIs for target behavioural symptoms in FTD
explanation.pearls: Preserved short-term memory with prominent behavioural change and frontal-anterior temporal atrophy is FTD until proven otherwise - and the memory drugs will not help.

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant choice in the elderly
stem:
A 77-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m2), hypertension on perindopril, osteoarthritis and mild urge incontinence presents with a 12-week history of low mood, anhedonia, early morning wakening at 4 am, poor appetite with 4 kg weight loss and passive suicidal ideation without plan. Her PHQ-9 score is 18. She has never taken an antidepressant.

A structured assessment excludes bipolar history, substance use, hypothyroidism (TSH normal), B12 deficiency and abnormal calcium. She lives alone but has daily contact with her daughter. She is worried about "tablets clashing" with her other medications and dislikes side effects. Her current medications are perindopril, atorvastatin, alendronate weekly, and paracetamol PRN.

data_table.Bloods: eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m2, sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), TSH within normal limits, B12 within normal limits, corrected calcium within normal limits.
data_table.Screening: PHQ-9 18/27, MoCA 27/30, no history of mania or hypomania.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line antidepressant?

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg daily titrated slowly with early sodium check
options.rationale: Sertraline is a preferred first-line SSRI in older adults because of a favourable interaction profile and mid-range half-life; starting low and going slow with an early sodium check addresses the SIADH risk that is highest in the first weeks of therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH: sertraline).

options.text: Amitriptyline 25 mg at night, titrated for mood and sleep
options.rationale: TCAs carry high anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension and cardiac toxicity risk in the elderly and are on STOPP; they are not first-line for late-life depression (Source: STOPP/START criteria; AMH: amitriptyline).

options.text: Paroxetine 20 mg daily, chosen for its short elimination half-life
options.rationale: Paroxetine has the highest anticholinergic burden among the SSRIs, prominent discontinuation syndrome and is not preferred in older adults (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily, chosen for its once-weekly formulation option
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has an active metabolite with a very long half-life, complicating dose adjustment and switching in older adults; it is not preferred first-line despite adherence benefits (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Venlafaxine 75 mg daily as an SNRI with dual serotonergic action
options.rationale: Venlafaxine can raise blood pressure at higher doses, has a discontinuation syndrome and SIADH risk similar to SSRIs; it is not preferred as first-line over sertraline in an older adult with hypertension and CKD (Source: AMH: venlafaxine).

explanation.summary: Preferred first-line antidepressants in older adults are sertraline, escitalopram (with dose cap 10 mg in over-65s due to QT signal) and mirtazapine (particularly if insomnia or poor appetite). TCAs and paroxetine are avoided because of anticholinergic burden. All serotonergic agents carry SIADH risk, which is highest in the first 2 to 4 weeks and warrants an early sodium check.
key_points: First-line: sertraline, escitalopram (10 mg cap over 65), mirtazapine
Avoid: TCAs (anticholinergic, cardiac), paroxetine (anticholinergic)
SIADH risk highest first 2 to 4 weeks
Start low, go slow, review at 2 to 4 weeks
explanation.pearls: "Start low, go slow, but do not go so slow you never get there" - undertreatment of late-life depression is common and dangerous.

subtopic_detail: SIADH from SSRI
stem:
A 76-year-old man was started on sertraline 25 mg daily for major depressive disorder three weeks ago, titrated to 50 mg after one week. He now presents to the GP with two days of headache, nausea and unsteadiness. His daughter says he has been slower and has been repeating himself over the last 48 hours. He is on perindopril 5 mg daily for hypertension and has no history of heart failure, cirrhosis or thiazide use.

On examination he is euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, JVP not raised, no oedema, and no postural change in blood pressure. Bloods today: sodium 124 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, cortisol and TSH within normal limits. Urine sodium is 62 mmol/L and urine osmolality is 480 mosmol/kg.

data_table.Serum: Sodium 124 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1, urea 4.8, creatinine 82 micromol/L, glucose 5.2, cortisol and TSH within normal limits.
data_table.Volume status: Euvolaemic, no oedema, no postural BP change.
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 50 mg daily (started 3 weeks ago), perindopril 5 mg daily.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Continue sertraline unchanged, add fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily to raise sodium
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is used for cerebral salt wasting, not for SSRI-induced SIADH; continuing the driver drug will not correct the underlying process (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Cease sertraline and admit for cautious fluid restriction with serial sodium checks
options.rationale: The clinical and biochemical picture fits SSRI-induced SIADH (euvolaemia, hyponatraemia, urine osmolality inappropriately high, urine sodium above 40 mmol/L, normal cortisol and TSH); the drug must be ceased and fluid restriction with careful sodium correction (rise no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 h) started to avoid osmotic demyelination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; AMH: sertraline).

options.text: Continue sertraline and give 3% hypertonic saline 500 mL over one hour for rapid correction
options.rationale: Bolus hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma) and even then in 100 to 150 mL aliquots; the target correction remains no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Cease perindopril as the most likely offending cause and continue sertraline
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are not a common cause of SIADH and the timing here strongly implicates the newly started SSRI, which is a well-recognised cause of SIADH in older adults (Source: AMH: sertraline).

options.text: Give 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over one hour and reassess
options.rationale: In SIADH, isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because the retained water outweighs the sodium load; fluid restriction is the mainstay, with hypertonic saline reserved for severe neurological symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: SSRIs are a common cause of SIADH in older adults, with risk highest in the first 2 to 4 weeks. Diagnosis requires euvolaemia, hyponatraemia, urine osmolality inappropriately concentrated (over 100 mosmol/kg with plasma hypotonicity), urine sodium above 40 mmol/L, and exclusion of cortisol and thyroid causes. Management is cessation of the drug and cautious fluid restriction; correction must not exceed 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
key_points: SSRI SIADH risk highest first 2 to 4 weeks
SIADH: euvolaemia, low serum Na, high urine osm, urine Na over 40
Correction cap: 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 h
Isotonic saline can worsen SIADH
explanation.pearls: A confused elder started on an SSRI in the last month: measure sodium before you measure the MMSE.

subtopic_detail: ECT indication in the elderly
stem:
An 80-year-old woman with severe major depressive disorder has lost 9 kg over three months and is now refusing to eat or drink. She has developed nihilistic delusions that her internal organs are rotting. She has already had adequate 6-week trials of sertraline (titrated to 200 mg) and mirtazapine (titrated to 45 mg) with negligible response, and augmentation with aripiprazole was ceased at 10 days for akathisia. She is now on the inpatient psychiatry ward under an involuntary treatment order.

Her PHQ-9 was 24 on admission and remains 22 today. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and postural hypotension. Bloods show sodium 128 mmol/L (SSRI-related), urea 9.6 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, and albumin 28 g/L. She has no pacemaker, no recent stroke, no unstable ischaemic heart disease and her most recent ECG showed sinus rhythm with QTc 440 ms.

data_table.Illness: Severe MDD with psychotic features (nihilistic), 3 months, food and fluid refusal, 9 kg weight loss.
data_table.Trials to date: Sertraline 200 mg 6 weeks minimal response; mirtazapine 45 mg 6 weeks minimal response; aripiprazole ceased for akathisia at day 10.
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 128 mmol/L, urea 9.6, creatinine 92, albumin 28 g/L.
data_table.Cardiac: No pacemaker, no recent stroke, ECG sinus rhythm, QTc 440 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Continue current pharmacotherapy for a further 4 to 6 weeks to allow full response
options.rationale: Adequate trials have already been completed; continuing failed pharmacotherapy with active food and fluid refusal in an older adult with hyponatraemia and hypoalbuminaemia is not appropriate (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Switch to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (phenelzine) after a two-week washout
options.rationale: MAOI trials in a physically compromised, dehydrated older adult with food refusal are not the safest or fastest option; ECT delivers response in days to weeks and is preferred over a washout-plus-MAOI approach in this severity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add lithium augmentation to mirtazapine targeting a level of 0.4 to 0.6 mmol/L
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is a reasonable strategy for less severe treatment-resistant depression but response takes weeks, and lithium risks toxicity when the patient is dehydrated with rising urea and known SIADH (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add nortriptyline to mirtazapine as a combination antidepressant strategy
options.rationale: Combining TCAs in a dehydrated older adult with postural hypotension is high-risk and slow-acting; ECT has a faster, safer profile in this severity of illness (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy as the treatment of choice in this presentation
options.rationale: Severe treatment-resistant depression with psychotic features, food and fluid refusal, and imminent physical risk in an older adult is a first-line indication for ECT, which has faster response times and higher remission rates than any pharmacological option in this presentation (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders; RANZCP ECT PPG).

explanation.summary: First-line ECT indications include severe depression with psychotic features, food/fluid refusal with medical compromise, high suicide risk, catatonia, and severe treatment-resistant depression. Older adults respond as well as or better than younger patients. Response rates around 70 to 80 percent, and older-adult remission is often faster than pharmacological alternatives.
key_points: First-line ECT: psychotic depression, food/fluid refusal, high risk, catatonia
Older adults have equal or superior response to ECT
Speed of response is the safety argument in medical compromise
Common adverse effects: transient memory disturbance, headache, myalgia
explanation.pearls: In severe depression with food refusal, ECT is not a last resort; it is often the safest first choice.

subtopic_detail: Highest-risk demographic
stem:
A 74-year-old man attends his GP two weeks after his wife of 48 years died. He lives alone in the family home, is retired, and has adult children interstate. He has hypertension, hearing loss, chronic back pain and a background of harmful alcohol use with 40 g of alcohol per day. He states his mood is "about what you'd expect" and denies suicidal ideation on direct questioning.

During the consultation you notice he has lost 3 kg since his last visit, has cancelled his upcoming knee surgery consultation and mentions in passing that he has given his fishing gear to his son "because I don't need it any more". His PHQ-9 is 14 with item 9 (thoughts of being better off dead) answered as "nearly every day". He has a licensed firearm at home.

data_table.Risk factors: Male, 74, recent bereavement, socially isolated, harmful alcohol use, chronic pain, hearing loss, firearm at home, giving away possessions, PHQ-9 item 9 positive daily.
data_table.Physical: Weight loss 3 kg since prior visit, cancelled elective surgery.
data_table.Denial: Denies active suicidal ideation on direct questioning.

lead_in: Which single statement about his suicide risk is correct?

options.text: Older men have the lowest completed suicide rate of any Australian age-sex group
options.rationale: This reverses the epidemiology; AIHW data show older men (particularly men aged 85 and above) have the highest completed suicide rate of any Australian age-sex group despite lower attempt rates (Source: AIHW Suicide and self-harm monitoring).

options.text: Direct denial of suicidal ideation reliably excludes suicide risk in the elderly
options.rationale: Older adults are less likely to disclose suicidal ideation on direct questioning; behavioural indicators (giving away possessions, cancelling future plans, PHQ-9 item 9 positive) may carry more weight than a single verbal denial (Source: RANZCP: Suicide and self-harm assessment).

options.text: Older Australian men have the highest completed suicide rate and this patient warrants urgent psychiatric input
options.rationale: AIHW data confirm men aged 85 and above have the highest age-specific suicide rate in Australia; this patient adds recent bereavement, isolation, alcohol misuse, chronic pain, disability, weight loss, cancelled plans, giving away possessions, firearm access and PHQ-9 item 9 daily to a highest-risk demographic (Source: AIHW Suicide and self-harm monitoring; RANZCP).

options.text: Attempt-to-completion ratio in older men is similar to that of adolescent females
options.rationale: Older men have the highest attempt-to-completion ratio in Australia, with methods of higher lethality and lower rescue rates; adolescent females have high attempt rates but much lower completion (Source: AIHW Suicide and self-harm monitoring).

options.text: A firearm at home does not modify suicide risk in an older man because access does not equate to use
options.rationale: Access to lethal means, particularly firearms, is one of the most modifiable risk factors for completed suicide and means restriction is a specific evidence-based intervention (Source: RANZCP: Suicide and self-harm assessment).

explanation.summary: Older Australian men, particularly those aged 85 and above, have the highest completed suicide rate of any age-sex group. They present with fewer verbal disclosures, higher method lethality and lower rescue rates. Key risk factors are bereavement, isolation, chronic pain and disability, alcohol misuse, cognitive change and access to lethal means. Behavioural indicators (giving away possessions, cancelling plans) carry additional weight when direct questioning is negative.
key_points: Men 85+ = highest AU age-specific suicide rate
Older men: fewer warnings, higher lethality
Modifiable: bereavement support, alcohol Rx, means restriction
PHQ-9 item 9 positive is not to be dismissed
explanation.pearls: In an older man in the weeks after bereavement, a passing comment about "not needing it any more" is a suicide risk assessment starting, not ending.

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal over 65
stem:
A 71-year-old man is admitted with a fractured neck of femur after a mechanical fall at home. On day 2 post-op he becomes tremulous, sweating, and mildly confused. His wife discloses that he has consumed a bottle of red wine each evening for the last 20 years and has not had a drink since admission 40 hours ago. His CIWA-Ar score is 14. He has hypertension on amlodipine, mild CKD (eGFR 54 mL/min/1.73 m2), and no cirrhosis on prior imaging.

He is haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and his post-operative pain is well controlled on paracetamol and low-dose oxycodone. Bloods show normal LFTs, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.9, glucose 6.0 mmol/L. He has no history of complicated withdrawal or seizures. The intern asks about the appropriate benzodiazepine choice given his age and renal function.

data_table.Withdrawal: CIWA-Ar 14 (tremor, sweating, mild confusion) at 40 h post last drink.
data_table.Bloods: LFTs within normal limits, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.9, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, eGFR 54 mL/min/1.73 m2.
data_table.History: Bottle of wine daily for 20 years, no prior seizures or DTs, no cirrhosis on prior imaging.

lead_in: Which benzodiazepine and dosing approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Diazepam 20 mg every hour by symptom-triggered dosing until CIWA-Ar below 10
options.rationale: Diazepam's active metabolites accumulate substantially in older adults and in even mild renal impairment, risking over-sedation, delirium and falls; a shorter-acting agent is preferred in patients over 65 (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction; AMH: diazepam).

options.text: Phenobarbital 130 mg intramuscularly as first-line treatment for withdrawal
options.rationale: Phenobarbital is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory withdrawal or ICU settings and is not a first-line agent for uncomplicated withdrawal on a general ward (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Chlordiazepoxide 50 mg four times daily for 5 days on a fixed schedule
options.rationale: Chlordiazepoxide is a long-acting agent with active metabolites and is avoided in older adults; fixed-dose schedules deliver more total benzodiazepine than symptom-triggered protocols and increase adverse effects (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Oxazepam 15 to 30 mg symptom-triggered on CIWA-Ar with regular review
options.rationale: Oxazepam and lorazepam are preferred in older adults, hepatic impairment and renal impairment because they are metabolised by glucuronidation without active metabolites; symptom-triggered dosing guided by CIWA-Ar minimises total exposure and reduces delirium risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Withhold benzodiazepines and manage with hydration and clonidine to avoid delirium risk
options.rationale: Withholding benzodiazepines in established withdrawal risks progression to withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens; benzodiazepines are the mainstay of treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

explanation.summary: In alcohol withdrawal in older adults or those with hepatic/renal impairment, oxazepam or lorazepam are preferred over diazepam and chlordiazepoxide because glucuronidation metabolism produces no active metabolites and prevents accumulation. Symptom-triggered dosing guided by CIWA-Ar delivers less total benzodiazepine than fixed-dose schedules and reduces adverse effects. Thiamine 100 mg IV or IM is given before any glucose to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
key_points: Over 65: oxazepam or lorazepam (no active metabolites)
Symptom-triggered dosing beats fixed schedule
Diazepam accumulates in older adults and renal impairment
Thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke's
explanation.pearls: Fluctuating confusion in a post-op elder without an obvious infective cause: ask about alcohol before ordering another septic screen.

subtopic_detail: Benzodiazepine deprescribing
stem:
A 78-year-old woman has been on temazepam 20 mg at night for 12 years, first prescribed after her husband died. She lives alone, mobilises with a four-wheel walker and had a fall three weeks ago requiring six stitches to her forehead. Her cognitive assessment today is MoCA 25 out of 30. She tells you she "needs" the temazepam to sleep and has been reluctant to change it. She has no formal diagnosis of insomnia disorder and denies mood or anxiety symptoms today.

Her medications are perindopril 5 mg mane, atorvastatin 20 mg nocte and temazepam 20 mg nocte. Her renal function is normal, LFTs are within normal limits and she has no known contraindication to sleep hygiene measures or short-term CBT-I. She has attended one bereavement counselling session in the past.

data_table.History: Temazepam 20 mg nocte for 12 years, recent fall with stitches, lives alone, MoCA 25/30.
data_table.Screen: No current mood or anxiety diagnosis; sleep-hygiene measures not previously trialled.
data_table.Bloods: eGFR over 60, LFTs within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to deprescribing?

options.text: Cease temazepam abruptly at the next appointment to avoid further fall risk
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of long-term benzodiazepines risks rebound insomnia, anxiety and (rarely) withdrawal seizures; the AU deprescribing guideline advises a gradual, negotiated taper (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing).

options.text: Switch to zopiclone 7.5 mg at night as a safer alternative for chronic use
options.rationale: Z-drugs share the fall, cognitive impairment and dependence profile of benzodiazepines in older adults and are on STOPP for the same reasons; switching does not address the problem (Source: STOPP/START criteria).

options.text: Continue temazepam indefinitely because 12 years of use makes deprescribing unsafe
options.rationale: Long duration of use is a reason to taper more slowly, not to continue indefinitely; ongoing use in an older adult with a recent fall carries clear net harm (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing).

options.text: Negotiate a gradual dose reduction of 10 to 25 percent every 2 to 4 weeks with CBT-I
options.rationale: AU deprescribing guidance advises a patient-negotiated taper of about 10 to 25 percent every 2 to 4 weeks (slower for very long-term users) with non-pharmacological insomnia strategies (sleep hygiene, CBT-I) as replacement, in an older adult with a recent fall on chronic benzodiazepine use (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing).

options.text: Add mirtazapine 30 mg at night to cover sleep and then cease temazepam within one week
options.rationale: Adding a second sedating drug in an older adult with a recent fall increases fall and sedation risk; the recommended pathway is a slow taper of the offending agent alongside non-pharmacological insomnia strategies (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Long-term benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults increase falls, fractures, cognitive impairment and delirium. Deprescribing pathways are negotiated with the patient, structured as gradual dose reductions (typically 10 to 25 percent every 2 to 4 weeks, slower for very long-term users) and paired with non-pharmacological insomnia strategies (sleep hygiene, CBT-I, stimulus control). Abrupt cessation risks rebound and seizures.
key_points: Taper 10 to 25% every 2 to 4 weeks, slower for years-long use
Non-pharmacological insomnia strategies replace the drug
Z-drugs are equivalent risk, not an escape
Patient negotiation matters for adherence
explanation.pearls: A fall on temazepam is not a reason to prescribe zopiclone; it is a reason to plan a taper.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and response
stem:
An 82-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 24 out of 30, retains capacity for financial and care decisions on formal assessment last month) attends the general practice with her son. He answers most of your questions on her behalf. She has come in for a repeat prescription and to "sort out the pension". You notice bruising in various stages of healing on her upper arms and a small circular burn on her forearm which she attributes to "being clumsy".

When you ask to see her alone, her son says "she gets confused, I need to stay". Her Medicare card and bank card are held by the son. She lives with him after selling her own home last year, with the proceeds transferred into his name to "help pay the bills". On direct questioning alone, she says she is "fine" but avoids eye contact and asks whether her son is going to be told what she says.

data_table.Cognitive status: MoCA 24/30, retains decision-making capacity on formal assessment 4 weeks ago.
data_table.Injuries: Bruising of upper arms in various stages of healing, small circular burn on forearm.
data_table.Financial: Sold own home in past year, proceeds transferred to son's name. Medicare and bank cards held by son.
data_table.Interaction: Son answers on her behalf, resists private interview.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Confront the son directly in the consultation about the injuries and financial concerns
options.rationale: Direct confrontation of a suspected perpetrator in the presence of the victim risks retaliation, loss of trust and further concealment; the priority is safe private interview and structured response (Source: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources).
source_refs: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources

options.text: Report to the police today as mandatory reporting of elder abuse applies in all Australian states
options.rationale: Elder abuse is not covered by a national mandatory reporting law equivalent to child protection; only aged care providers have mandatory reporting duties under the Aged Care Act (SIRS scheme). Community elder abuse response is consent-based when the person has capacity (Source: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources).
source_refs: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources

options.text: Refer directly to the public guardian for financial substitute decision-making today
options.rationale: She retains decision-making capacity on formal assessment; a guardianship application without her consent and without capacity loss is inappropriate and paternalistic (Source: Office of the Public Advocate).

options.text: Complete the repeat prescription and address her concerns at the next annual review
options.rationale: Multiple concurrent physical and financial abuse indicators demand action at this visit, not deferral; deferral risks escalation and further injury (Source: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources).
source_refs: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources

options.text: Interview her alone and, with her consent, contact the state elder abuse helpline
options.rationale: A capacitous older person with multiple abuse indicators (physical injuries in various stages of healing, financial control, thwarted private communication) requires a private interview to enable disclosure, a structured assessment, and a coordinated response through the state elder abuse helpline; her retained capacity means her consent is paramount and mandatory reporting frameworks differ from child protection (Source: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources; Elder Abuse Action Australia).
source_refs: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources

explanation.summary: Elder abuse can be physical, financial, emotional, sexual, neglect or a mix. Warning signs include unexplained injuries in various stages of healing, controlled communication, financial transfers, thwarted private interviews and social isolation. In Australia, community elder abuse response is consent-based when the older person has capacity; mandatory reporting under the Aged Care Act (SIRS) applies to aged care providers, not GPs in the community. Each state has an elder abuse helpline (e.g. 1800 ELDERHelp - 1800 353 374 - national line routes to state services).
key_points: Private interview first, capacity-based response
AU community elder abuse response is consent-based
SIRS mandatory reporting is aged-care-provider specific
State elder abuse helpline is core referral
explanation.pearls: When someone else answers every question and holds the bank card, ask to see the patient alone before you print anything.

sources.label: RACGP Elder Abuse Aged Care resources

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic risk decision in vascular dementia with recent stroke
stem:
An 84-year-old man with vascular dementia (MMSE 16) is admitted from a residential aged care facility with escalating aggression: he has struck two staff and another resident in the last week, and non-pharmacological measures over four weeks (structured routine, one-to-one, redirection, tailored music) have failed. A full reversible-cause workup is negative. His MRI three months ago showed multiple bilateral small-vessel infarcts and one small right middle cerebral artery cortical infarct sustained six weeks ago from which he has largely recovered motor function.

He is on aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, perindopril 5 mg and no antipsychotic. His current QTc is 460 ms. His son (substitute decision maker) asks for a plan. He has no history of Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies. He weighs 62 kg and eGFR is 55 mL/min/1.73 m2.

data_table.Behaviour: Aggression with harm to staff and resident, 4 weeks of failed non-pharmacological plan, reversible-cause workup negative.
data_table.Cerebrovascular: Multiple bilateral small-vessel infarcts; right MCA cortical infarct 6 weeks ago.
data_table.Cardiac/renal: QTc 460 ms, eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m2, weight 62 kg.
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, perindopril 5 mg.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily with informed consent covering stroke and mortality risk
options.rationale: When non-pharmacological measures have genuinely failed and there is a documented risk of harm to self or others, risperidone remains the AU PBS-listed BPSD antipsychotic option even in vascular dementia; the elevated cerebrovascular and mortality risk (particularly relevant in this patient with recent infarct) must be explicitly addressed in consent, the dose kept minimum-effective, QTc rechecked, and formal review at 6 to 12 weeks planned (Source: PBS/RPBS Risperidone BPSD listing; RANZCP FPOP BPSD Guidelines; TGA cerebrovascular warning).

options.text: Prescribe olanzapine 5 mg orally at night as the safest antipsychotic option given the recent stroke
options.rationale: The cerebrovascular signal is a class effect for both risperidone and olanzapine and olanzapine additionally has substantial anticholinergic burden and metabolic risk; it is not the preferred AU BPSD antipsychotic and is not "safer" post-stroke (Source: TGA antipsychotic cerebrovascular warning; RANZCP FPOP BPSD Guidelines).

options.text: Prescribe haloperidol 1 mg twice daily as a non-atypical option that carries no cerebrovascular signal
options.rationale: Haloperidol also carries mortality and cerebrovascular event signal in dementia and has a higher extrapyramidal burden; it is not preferred over the AU PBS-listed atypical for chronic BPSD (Source: TGA antipsychotic cerebrovascular warning; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 2 mg twice daily as an antipsychotic alternative to avoid cerebrovascular risk
options.rationale: Diazepam is on STOPP for older adults, worsens cognition, increases fall risk, and does not treat aggression in dementia; substituting it for a needed antipsychotic in a risk-of-harm scenario is not appropriate (Source: STOPP/START criteria).

options.text: Continue non-pharmacological measures for another 12 weeks without any medication change
options.rationale: Four weeks of a structured non-pharmacological plan has already failed and there is active risk of harm to staff and residents; continuing indefinitely without pharmacological input is not consistent with the AU risk-of-harm indication for time-limited antipsychotic use (Source: RANZCP FPOP BPSD Guidelines).

explanation.summary: The TGA cerebrovascular warning and increased all-cause mortality signal apply to all antipsychotics in dementia. This does not remove risperidone as an option when non-pharmacological measures have failed and there is risk of harm - it raises the bar for consent (substitute decision maker informed of stroke and mortality risk, particularly relevant with recent infarct), for dose (start 0.25 mg twice daily, minimum-effective titration to a maximum of 2 mg daily), for physiological safety (recheck QTc, review renal function) and for review (6 to 12 weeks with intent to withdraw). The competing pull between "do not prescribe post-stroke" and "must treat imminent risk-of-harm" is what makes this a stop-and-think choice.
key_points: TGA cerebrovascular warning applies to all antipsychotics
Risperidone is the PBS-listed BPSD agent (max 2 mg/day)
Non-atypical alternatives share the risk signal
Consent must explicitly cover stroke and mortality risk
explanation.pearls: In a recent stroke plus dementia plus aggression, the answer is not "avoid antipsychotics" but "use the smallest dose of the best-evidenced agent, with the most explicit consent and the tightest review".

subtopic_detail: EPDS interpretation and next step
stem:
A 31-year-old woman attends her general practice in suburban Adelaide for a 6-week postnatal check. Her first baby was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth at 40 weeks and is exclusively breastfed and growing well. The practice nurse has administered the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) in the waiting room and the total score is 15. On item 10 (self-harm) she scored 0.

She tells you the last three weeks have felt "grey", she cries most days, sleep is broken beyond what the baby demands, and she finds no pleasure in things that previously interested her. She denies suicidal or infanticidal ideas, has no psychotic features, and eats reasonably. Her partner is supportive and she has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder. Basic postnatal examination and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.History: 6 weeks postpartum, breastfeeding, no bipolar history, no psychosis, no suicidal/infanticidal ideas
data_table.Examination: Postnatal examination within normal limits; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that this represents normal baby blues resolving spontaneously and arrange telephone review with the practice nurse in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Baby blues resolve by day 10-14 and do not produce an EPDS of 15; her symptoms have persisted for 3 weeks at 6 weeks postpartum. (Source: Beyond Blue COPE perinatal guideline).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Repeat the EPDS in 2 weeks before making any diagnostic decision or committing to psychological or pharmacological management
options.rationale: An EPDS of at least 13 with 3 weeks of pervasive symptoms already meets the threshold for further clinical assessment and treatment planning today; delaying loses treatment weeks. Would rarely be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Undertake structured clinical assessment for perinatal depression and commence psychological therapy, with sertraline added if moderate or worse
options.rationale: The COPE Australian perinatal guideline treats an EPDS score of at least 13 as a positive screen requiring a structured clinical assessment (not a diagnosis in itself). With 3 weeks of pervasive anhedonia and low mood at 6 weeks postpartum, moderate perinatal depression is likely; stepped care starts with psychological therapy (CBT or IPT) with sertraline added for moderate or severe presentations because sertraline has the lowest relative infant dose in breast milk (Source: COPE; MotherToBaby Australia; AMH).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in lactation factsheet

options.text: Refer urgently to the acute mental health team for same-day psychiatric review and consideration of inpatient admission to a mother-baby unit
options.rationale: Acute team referral is reserved for suicidal or infanticidal ideation, psychotic features, or severe functional collapse; she has none of these. Would rarely be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Commence paroxetine 20 mg orally daily as first-line pharmacotherapy and continue breastfeeding without further specialist monitoring
options.rationale: Paroxetine is not preferred in breastfeeding when a naive start is being made; sertraline is favoured because of its very low relative infant dose. Would never be correct as first-line in a breastfeeding woman (Source: MotherToBaby Australia; AMH).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in lactation factsheet

explanation.summary: An EPDS score of at least 13 is a positive screen for perinatal depression per the COPE Australian guideline and triggers a structured clinical assessment and stepped-care management, not simple reassurance or repeat screening.
key_points: EPDS at least 13 = positive screen; EPDS 10-12 = borderline (repeat in 2-4 weeks)
Baby blues peak day 3-5 and resolve by day 10-14
Item 10 = self-harm; any positive score triggers immediate safety assessment
Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding (lowest relative infant dose)
Screen for bipolar and psychosis before starting any antidepressant
explanation.pearls: The EPDS screens for anxiety as well as depression; a moderate score with prominent anxious items should still be taken as a positive screen. In context: perinatal depression at 6 weeks postpartum with a screen-positive EPDS deserves the same rigour as any new episode of major depression, calibrated to the safety of the mother-infant dyad (Source: COPE).

sources.label: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in lactation factsheet

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis - urgent disposition
stem:
A 28-year-old primipara is brought to a metropolitan emergency department 9 days postpartum by her mother. Her pregnancy and vaginal birth were uncomplicated. Over the last 48 hours she has slept less than 3 hours per night, become progressively agitated, and now insists that her baby's cry contains coded messages from her deceased grandmother telling her the baby must be "purified by water". She is fluctuating between elated and tearful within minutes.

She has a personal history of bipolar I disorder (last episode 4 years ago on lithium, ceased 8 months preconception with psychiatric agreement) and a maternal history of postpartum psychosis. On examination she is oriented but distractible with pressured speech; the baby is with her partner and appears well and feeding. Vital signs are within normal limits. Routine bloods including urea, electrolytes, creatinine, LFTs, calcium, TSH, glucose and CRP are within normal limits and urine drug screen is negative.

data_table.Timeline: Day 9 postpartum; 48 h agitation, insomnia, delusions, mood lability
data_table.Psychiatric history: Bipolar I, last episode 4 years ago; mother had postpartum psychosis
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, corrected Ca, TSH, glucose, CRP within normal limits; UDS negative
data_table.Infant: With partner, feeding, no injuries reported

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home on olanzapine 10 mg orally nightly, provide a written safety plan, and arrange acute community mental health team review the following morning
options.rationale: Community follow-up cannot manage the acute infanticide and suicide risk of postpartum psychosis; delirium has been excluded and admission is required. (Source: RANZCP perinatal position statement).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Admit as a psychiatric emergency (Mother-Baby Unit preferred where available), commence olanzapine, and reintroduce lithium after baseline bloods
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with substantial suicide and infanticide risk. RANZCP and COPE recommend admission to a specialist Mother-Baby Unit where available (or the nearest inpatient bed with arrangements to maintain the mother-infant relationship if no MBU) with an antipsychotic (olanzapine is commonly used) and reintroduction of a mood stabiliser such as lithium; ECT is considered for treatment resistance or life-threatening severity (Source: RANZCP; COPE; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture and MRI brain to exclude autoimmune or viral encephalitis before initiating any psychiatric admission or antipsychotic therapy
options.rationale: Organic screen is normal and the clinical picture (personal and family bipolar history, day 9 postpartum, characteristic mood-congruent psychosis) is classical for postpartum psychosis; further imaging is not needed before admission. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily, refer to community psychology for postnatal depression, and arrange partner-supervised follow-up in three days
options.rationale: Sertraline monotherapy can precipitate mania in bipolar patients and does not treat acute psychosis; the presentation is not depression. (Source: RANZCP; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Advise the partner and grandmother to supervise her at home for 24 hours, remove access to means, and represent immediately if symptoms worsen at all
options.rationale: Home supervision is inappropriate for postpartum psychosis regardless of a supportive partner. (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis in a woman with bipolar I and a positive family history is a psychiatric emergency requiring urgent inpatient admission (ideally a Mother-Baby Unit) with antipsychotic and mood stabiliser therapy.
key_points: Peak onset days 3-14 postpartum, often abrupt
Personal or family history of bipolar or postpartum psychosis raises risk to about 1 in 2 in some cohorts
Suicide and infanticide risk is high and both dyad members need safeguarding
First-line: antipsychotic (often olanzapine) plus mood stabiliser (lithium if not breastfeeding a preterm or unwell infant; olanzapine or quetiapine if breastfeeding is prioritised)
ECT is highly effective and safe for severe or treatment-resistant cases
explanation.pearls: Always ask about family history of postpartum psychosis in any pregnant or newly postpartum woman with a mood disorder; it is one of the strongest predictors of recurrence. In context: rapid inpatient stabilisation preserves the mother-infant relationship better than delayed community care because untreated psychosis erodes early attachment and safety (Source: RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

subtopic_detail: Bipolar in pregnancy - lithium in the first trimester
stem:
A 33-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder that has been stable for 5 years on lithium modified-release 900 mg orally nightly (steady-state serum lithium 0.7 mmol/L) attends her GP at 6 weeks gestation after a positive home pregnancy test. Her last three episodes off lithium were severe manias, one requiring involuntary admission; two prior trials of valproate and lamotrigine each failed to prevent relapse within 4 months. She is otherwise well, plans to continue the pregnancy, and asks what to do about her medication.

She tells you she has read that lithium causes heart defects and wants to stop today. Renal function, thyroid function, and corrected calcium are within normal limits. Fetal ultrasound and dating are booked.

data_table.Psychiatric history: Bipolar I, stable 5 y on lithium; two prior alternative mood stabilisers ineffective
data_table.Current medication: Lithium MR 900 mg nocte, steady-state level 0.7 mmol/L
data_table.Investigations: UEC, TSH, corrected calcium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her lithium in the first trimester?

options.text: Continue lithium, arrange fetal cardiac ultrasound at 18-22 weeks, monitor serum lithium every 4 weeks with dose adjustment as pregnancy progresses
options.rationale: The absolute first-trimester risk of Ebstein anomaly with lithium is small (around 1 in 1000-2000, roughly 10-20 times baseline of 1 in 20 000). Her relapse risk without a mood stabiliser is very high with catastrophic consequences (previous severe mania, two failed alternatives). MotherToBaby Australia and RANZCP advise that continuing lithium is appropriate when alternatives have failed, with fetal cardiac imaging at 18-22 weeks and lithium monitoring every 4 weeks (more often in the third trimester because volume of distribution rises) (Source: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet; RANZCP; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Stop lithium abruptly today because of the risk of Ebstein anomaly, switch to sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily, and rely on obstetric monitoring alone
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation carries about a 50% mania relapse risk within weeks; valproate is teratogenic (neural tube defects) and contraindicated in pregnancy under the pregnancy prevention program. (Source: AMH; MotherToBaby Australia).

options.text: Cross-taper lithium to lamotrigine 200 mg orally daily over 4 weeks with weekly review and no additional fetal cardiac imaging beyond the routine anatomy scan
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has already failed to prevent relapse in this patient; changing to a known-ineffective agent risks severe mania. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Continue lithium but empirically reduce the dose to 450 mg nocte to lower fetal exposure, without a maternal serum lithium level to guide the change
options.rationale: Empirically halving the dose neither meaningfully reduces first-trimester teratogenic risk (which is dose-related but the risk of a subtherapeutic level and relapse dominates) nor is guided by levels; dose changes should be driven by serum lithium. Would rarely be correct (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

options.text: Stop lithium and rely on close psychiatric monitoring alone for the first trimester, restarting after 12 weeks only if she remains well and asymptomatic
options.rationale: Monitoring without prophylaxis in a patient with a high relapse rate and two failed alternatives exposes both mother and fetus to the far greater harm of untreated severe mania. (Source: RANZCP; MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: For a woman with severe bipolar I on lithium who has failed alternatives, the risk of untreated mania in pregnancy exceeds the small absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly; lithium is continued with fetal cardiac imaging at 18-22 weeks and serial level monitoring.
key_points: First-trimester lithium risk of Ebstein anomaly is about 1 in 1000-2000 (baseline 1 in 20 000)
Fetal cardiac ultrasound at 18-22 weeks is recommended for lithium-exposed pregnancies
Serum lithium falls in the second and third trimesters as volume of distribution rises; monitor 4-weekly then 2-weekly late pregnancy
Withhold or reduce lithium 24-48 h before planned delivery to avoid neonatal toxicity, restart postpartum
Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy (neural tube defects, later neurodevelopment)
explanation.pearls: The Ebstein statistic is a good example of relative-risk optics that ignore base rates; the absolute risk is small and the counter-risk of untreated severe mania is large. In context: shared decision-making about pregnancy and lithium requires framing risk in absolute terms and against the alternative of untreated illness (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

sources.label: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

subtopic_detail: Lithium in breastfeeding
stem:
A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is 3 weeks postpartum after a healthy term birth. She restarted lithium modified-release 900 mg nocte on day 2 postpartum on your advice and is currently well, with a maternal serum lithium of 0.7 mmol/L. Her infant is breastfeeding well, growing along the 50th percentile, and appears alert and hydrated.

Her partner has read online that lithium is "absolutely contraindicated" in breastfeeding and is anxious. She would strongly prefer to continue breastfeeding. The infant has no dysmorphism, no jitteriness, and no poor feeding; a paediatric review the previous day was unremarkable.

data_table.Maternal medication: Lithium MR 900 mg nocte; maternal serum Li 0.7 mmol/L
data_table.Infant: Term, 3 weeks old, feeding well, growing along 50th percentile, no jitteriness or lethargy
data_table.Family concern: Partner concerned about breastfeeding on lithium

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise she must stop breastfeeding immediately and switch to formula because lithium is absolutely contraindicated in lactation regardless of maternal preference
options.rationale: Lithium in breastfeeding is not absolutely contraindicated; it is a shared decision requiring monitoring, and abrupt cessation has psychological costs. (Source: MotherToBaby Australia lithium factsheet).

options.text: Continue breastfeeding but empirically reduce her maternal lithium dose to 450 mg nocte to reduce infant exposure and repeat maternal levels in a fortnight
options.rationale: Empirical maternal dose reduction risks maternal relapse and does not reliably lower infant serum lithium; the standard is monitor not empirically reduce. Would rarely be correct (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

options.text: Cross-taper her from lithium to olanzapine 15 mg nocte over 4 weeks so she can breastfeed safely, and cease all lithium once olanzapine is established
options.rationale: Olanzapine is not the preferred mood stabiliser for lithium-responsive bipolar I with a history of severe mania; switching a well patient introduces relapse risk without necessity. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Continue breastfeeding with informed consent, monitor infant serum lithium, UEC, and TSH at 2-4 weeks, and educate parents on signs of infant toxicity
options.rationale: Contemporary Australian sources (MotherToBaby Australia, RANZCP) accept breastfeeding on lithium with informed consent and paediatric involvement, provided the infant is term, healthy, and can be monitored. Infant serum lithium is usually 10-50% of maternal, and periodic infant lithium, renal, and thyroid function testing plus parental education on jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, and dehydration is the standard approach (Source: MotherToBaby Australia; RANZCP; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Recommend she express and discard breast milk for 4 hours after each lithium dose and then feed the infant to reduce peak lithium exposure through milk
options.rationale: Pump-and-dump timing does not appreciably reduce infant lithium exposure because lithium has a long half-life and is not confined to a peak; this is not a recognised strategy. (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

explanation.summary: Lithium in breastfeeding is acceptable in a well, term infant with monitoring; the older "absolutely contraindicated" teaching has been superseded by Australian and international perinatal guidance.
key_points: Infant serum lithium typically 10-50% of maternal
Monitor infant serum lithium, UEC, TSH at 2-4 weeks and then periodically
Educate parents on infant toxicity: jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, dehydration
Highest-risk periods: hot weather, gastroenteritis, prolonged interfeed intervals
Weigh benefits of breastfeeding against benefits of maternal mood stability
explanation.pearls: Shared decision-making trumps blanket rules in perinatal psychopharmacology; the older lithium-in-breastfeeding taboo caused avoidable relapse. In context: preserving both maternal stability and breastfeeding is achievable in most well term dyads with appropriate monitoring (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

sources.label: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

subtopic_detail: SSRI selection in pregnancy
stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 7 weeks gestation attends her GP with an escalating major depressive episode. This is a planned first pregnancy. She has a 4-year history of recurrent moderate to severe depression previously stabilised on paroxetine 20 mg orally daily, which she stopped 3 months before conception on her own initiative. She now reports 3 weeks of low mood, early morning waking, poor appetite, and thoughts that life is "not worth it" without a specific plan. She is not psychotic and has no bipolar history. Basic bloods and thyroid function are within normal limits.

She is willing to restart medication but has read that antidepressants "cause heart defects" in the first trimester and asks what is safest.

data_table.History: Recurrent MDD, 4 y; stopped paroxetine 3 months preconception
data_table.Current episode: 3 weeks moderate-severe depression, passive suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart paroxetine 20 mg orally daily because she previously responded to it, and refer for structured psychological therapy in parallel over 6 weeks
options.rationale: Paroxetine is best avoided if a naive start can be made in the first trimester because of a small increase in relative risk of cardiac malformations reported in several cohorts; sertraline is a safer restart in a woman not currently on paroxetine. Would rarely be correct at 7 weeks with no current exposure (Source: MotherToBaby Australia; RANZCP).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily and refer for structured psychological therapy such as CBT or interpersonal therapy
options.rationale: Sertraline is the SSRI of choice when starting or restarting antidepressant therapy in the first trimester because the reproductive safety data are the most reassuring and it also has the lowest relative infant dose in breast milk, providing continuity for postpartum feeding. Combined with structured psychological therapy this represents best-practice moderate-severe perinatal depression care (Source: COPE; MotherToBaby Australia; RANZCP).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Withhold pharmacotherapy for the first trimester and reassess mood, appetite, and suicidal ideation at 13 weeks with a repeat EPDS at that visit
options.rationale: Untreated moderate-severe depression in pregnancy carries meaningful risks (poor engagement with antenatal care, low birth weight, preterm birth, postpartum depression) and passive suicidal ideation is present. Would rarely be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.text: Commence venlafaxine 75 mg extended release orally daily as first-line perinatal antidepressant therapy with a plan to titrate up in 2 weeks if needed
options.rationale: SNRIs are second-line for perinatal depression; there is more experience with SSRIs and sertraline in particular. Would rarely be correct as first-line (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Refer urgently for electroconvulsive therapy as the safest treatment in pregnancy given her passive suicidal ideation and prior antidepressant responsiveness
options.rationale: ECT is safe in pregnancy but reserved for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant depression and severe suicidality with imminent risk; it is not first-line for moderate-severe depression that has not had a medication trial. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI when initiating or restarting antidepressant treatment in early pregnancy because reproductive safety data are most reassuring and continuity into breastfeeding is straightforward.
key_points: Sertraline: first-line SSRI in pregnancy and breastfeeding (low relative infant dose)
Paroxetine: avoid naive start in first trimester (small excess risk of cardiac malformations); may continue if already stable and switching risks relapse
Fluoxetine: long half-life, more accumulation in neonate
Neonatal adaptation syndrome (jitteriness, hypoglycaemia, respiratory distress) can follow third-trimester SSRI exposure, usually self-limited
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn: absolute risk small (about 3 per 1000 exposed vs 1-2 per 1000 unexposed)
explanation.pearls: The perinatal safety story of SSRIs has been overstated in lay media; framing risks in absolute terms and against the risks of untreated depression is central to informed consent. In context: sertraline is a reasonable default in most perinatal MDD presentations because it also carries safely into breastfeeding (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

sources.label: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

subtopic_detail: ECT in pregnancy - severe depression with suicidality
stem: A 34-year-old woman at 24 weeks gestation is admitted involuntarily under the Mental Health Act to a tertiary maternal mental health unit with severe depression. She has psychomotor retardation, has stopped eating and drinking for the past 3 days requiring intravenous fluids, believes her fetus "is already dead" despite normal cardiotocograph tracings, and has begun to endorse a specific plan of self-strangulation. Adequate trials of sertraline (200 mg) and mirtazapine (45 mg) for 6 and 8 weeks respectively during this pregnancy have failed. Obstetric assessment shows a well fetus of appropriate size for gestational age. Bloods including urea, electrolytes, creatinine, LFTs and TSH are within normal limits.

data_table.Presentation: Severe MDD with psychotic features, active suicidal plan, food refusal 3 days
data_table.Prior treatment: Sertraline 200 mg 6 wks; mirtazapine 45 mg 8 wks - both ineffective
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Add olanzapine 10 mg orally nightly to her current sertraline and mirtazapine, continue involuntary care, and reassess mood, suicidality, and oral intake in 4 weeks
options.rationale: A further 4-week medication trial is unsafe in the face of imminent suicidality, food refusal, and psychotic depression, and delays a definitive treatment. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Add lithium 750 mg nocte as augmentation, continue current antidepressants at maximum tolerated doses, and reassess her mood and suicidality over the next 2 weeks
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation would not act quickly enough for imminent suicidality and food refusal at 24 weeks; ECT is definitive. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Proceed with electroconvulsive therapy after joint obstetric-anaesthetic assessment, with left lateral tilt, airway protection, and pre- and post-treatment fetal monitoring
options.rationale: ECT is safe across all trimesters of pregnancy and is indicated for severe depression with psychotic features, active suicidality, treatment resistance, or food refusal endangering mother or fetus. Standard obstetric precautions apply: joint obstetric-anaesthetic assessment, left lateral tilt to prevent aortocaval compression, non-particulate antacid, avoidance of hyperventilation, and fetal heart rate monitoring pre- and post-ECT after viability (Source: RANZCP ECT clinical memorandum; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Commence intranasal esketamine 84 mg twice weekly as a rapid-acting antidepressant, continue current antidepressants, and monitor blood pressure after each dose
options.rationale: Esketamine is not established in pregnancy and PBS access does not cover this indication; safer, better-evidenced options exist. (Source: AMH).

options.text: Defer any definitive treatment change until after delivery, maintain her current sertraline and mirtazapine regimen, and continue one-to-one nursing observation
options.rationale: Deferring treatment risks maternal death and fetal loss; severe untreated depression in pregnancy is itself high-risk. (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: ECT is safe and effective across pregnancy for severe treatment-resistant depression, psychotic depression, active suicidality, and food refusal, provided obstetric-anaesthetic precautions are observed.
key_points: ECT indications in pregnancy: severe suicidality, psychotic depression, catatonia, food refusal, treatment resistance, severe mania endangering pregnancy
Precautions: joint obstetric and anaesthetic assessment, left lateral tilt after 20 weeks, non-particulate antacid, avoid hyperventilation, fetal monitoring after viability
Response typically seen after 4-6 treatments; maintenance considered if history of relapse
Common side effects: retrograde amnesia (mostly reversible), transient headache, myalgia
explanation.pearls: ECT is often the safest treatment for the fetus in severe maternal illness because it avoids ongoing systemic drug exposure. In context: framing ECT as an active safety choice for the dyad, rather than a last resort, aligns with contemporary RANZCP practice (Source: RANZCP ECT memorandum).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management in ED
stem:
A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police under mental health apprehension powers after 5 days of progressively pressured speech, minimal sleep, spending $12 000 on cryptocurrency, and grandiose delusions of being a "chosen prophet". He has a known diagnosis of bipolar I disorder and admits to stopping his lithium 3 weeks ago. He is not on any other regular medication.

He is oriented but distractible with flight of ideas and paces the interview room. He denies suicidal or homicidal ideation and has no active plan of harm. He accepts oral medication. Vital signs: pulse 108 bpm, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 C. Urea, electrolytes, creatinine, LFTs, TSH, and urine drug screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Presentation: 5 days manic symptoms; pressured speech, grandiose delusions, no suicidal or homicidal intent
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, TSH, UDS within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Recommence lithium modified release 750 mg orally nocte as monotherapy, offer oral lorazepam 1 mg for sleep, and reassess mania severity clinically in 48 hours
options.rationale: Lithium monotherapy takes 1-2 weeks to reach therapeutic serum levels and clinical effect; acute mania needs faster tranquillising cover. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Give a single intramuscular droperidol 10 mg immediately for tranquillisation, physically restrain until sedated, and admit to a psychiatric intensive care unit
options.rationale: Parenteral rapid tranquillisation is reserved for patients unable to accept oral medication or with imminent behavioural risk; he is accepting oral medication and is not physically aggressive. Would rarely be correct (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance clinical care standard).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 1000 mg orally daily as monotherapy and discharge with community mental health follow-up in 3 days, with a partner-supervised safety plan
options.rationale: Discharge is inappropriate for acute mania under mental health apprehension with grandiose delusions and financial risk; valproate monotherapy also lacks the rapid tranquillising effect. (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Commence oral olanzapine 10 mg or quetiapine 400 mg, reintroduce lithium once renal function is confirmed, and offer oral lorazepam 1-2 mg for agitation
options.rationale: Combination therapy of a mood stabiliser plus an SGA is more effective than either alone in acute mania; the SGA delivers rapid antimanic and tranquillising effect while lithium re-establishes prophylaxis. Oral lorazepam is used for adjunctive sedation when required. The RANZCP mood disorders CPG and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic support this stepped approach (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Commence carbamazepine 400 mg orally twice daily with diazepam 10 mg orally three times daily and discharge with community psychiatric follow-up in one week
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is a third-line antimanic; diazepam accumulates and is not preferred for procedural sedation in acute mania (lorazepam is preferred for consistent kinetics). Would rarely be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Acute mania is managed with combination therapy: a rapidly-acting SGA plus a mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate as appropriate), with adjunctive lorazepam for agitation, and admission where risk warrants.
key_points: First-line combination: SGA (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole) plus mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate)
Lorazepam preferred over diazepam for adjunctive tranquillisation (no active metabolites, predictable half-life)
Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women of reproductive potential unless the pregnancy prevention program is met
Screen for substance-induced mania (UDS) before attributing to bipolar
Admit under the Mental Health Act if insight is absent and there is risk to self, others, or reputation/finances
explanation.pearls: Reputation and financial catastrophe count as harm for the purposes of civil commitment assessment. In context: rapid combination therapy shortens time to remission and length of stay compared with monotherapy in acute mania (Source: RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders
NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus NMS versus anticholinergic
stem:
A 42-year-old man presents to a regional emergency department 6 hours after being started on tramadol 50 mg orally four times daily by his GP for acute back pain. His regular medications include venlafaxine 150 mg extended release daily (for depression, stable 2 years) and selegiline that was recently prescribed by a neurologist. He is agitated, sweating profusely, and complaining of jaw clenching.

On examination he is diaphoretic, has spontaneous bilateral lower limb clonus on ankle dorsiflexion (right greater than left), brisk reflexes throughout, hyperactive bowel sounds, and dilated but reactive pupils. Vital signs: pulse 128 bpm, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.2 C. He is oriented but restless.

data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, spontaneous lower limb clonus R>L, hyperreflexia, hyperactive bowel sounds, dilated reactive pupils, jaw clenching
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine 150 mg XR, selegiline (recent), tramadol 50 mg qid (started 6 h ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, stop the offending antipsychotic, provide aggressive cooling, and admit to intensive care for supportive care
options.rationale: NMS produces lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, and a subacute onset (usually days) and is triggered by dopamine antagonists, which he is not on. The clonus, hyperreflexia, and rapid onset after serotonergic loading argue against NMS. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; RANZCP).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Anticholinergic toxicity; give IV physostigmine 1 mg with cardiac monitoring, provide aggressive cooling and IV fluids, and admit for continued observation overnight
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxicity produces dry skin, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention, and unreactive dilated pupils. He is diaphoretic with hyperactive bowel sounds and reactive pupils. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

options.text: Sympathomimetic toxicity from occult stimulant use; obtain a urine drug screen, give IV benzodiazepines for agitation, and manage supportively with cooling and fluids
options.rationale: Sympathomimetic toxicity does not classically produce clonus and hyperreflexia; his medications and the temporal relationship to tramadol point to serotonergic causation. Would rarely be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

options.text: Panic attack with concurrent fever from a viral illness; give oral lorazepam 1 mg, provide paracetamol for the fever, reassess in an hour, and discharge if settled
options.rationale: Panic does not produce clonus, hyperreflexia, or temperature 39.2 C, and the medication sequence is diagnostic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

options.text: Serotonin syndrome; cease all serotonergic agents, provide aggressive cooling and IV fluids, give benzodiazepines for agitation, consider cyproheptadine if severe
options.rationale: The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria are satisfied (spontaneous clonus in the presence of a serotonergic agent) and the classical triad of neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia), autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, hyperthermia), and altered mental state is present after a serotonergic loading event. Australian toxicology practice is to cease serotonergic agents, provide supportive care with active cooling, generous IV fluids, and benzodiazepines for agitation and muscle activity; cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2A antagonist) is considered for persisting or severe symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; AMH).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is diagnosed by the Hunter criteria (serotonergic agent plus clonus, agitation with sweating, tremor with hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with hyperthermia); management is cessation, cooling, fluids, benzodiazepines, and cyproheptadine for severe cases.
key_points: Onset within hours of a serotonergic dose change; neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia) is the key differentiator from NMS
MAOI + serotonergic (tramadol, SSRI, SNRI, pethidine) combinations carry the highest risk
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, days-scale onset, dopamine antagonist trigger
Anticholinergic toxidrome: hot dry red skin, unreactive dilated pupils, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention
Malignant hyperthermia: inhalational anaesthetic or succinylcholine trigger, family history
explanation.pearls: Tramadol is a common inadvertent trigger of serotonin syndrome because it combines opioid and serotonergic activity; check for MAOIs and SSRIs before prescribing. In context: distinguishing the hyperthermic toxidromes at the bedside prevents lethal misdiagnosis and dangerous treatments (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Rapid tranquillisation choice in ED
stem: A 38-year-old man with a known diagnosis of schizophrenia is brought to a large metropolitan emergency department by police under mental health apprehension powers after threatening staff at a supported accommodation service. In the ED he is pacing, shouting at unseen figures, refusing to speak with staff, and has just struck a chair against the wall. Verbal de-escalation by a psychiatric nurse and a security officer for 10 minutes has been unsuccessful, and he refuses all oral medication. His weight is estimated at 90 kg, he has no known allergies, and there is no clear history of QT prolongation. Point-of-care ECG is not immediately available. He has not taken alcohol or benzodiazepines in the past 24 hours per accompanying support worker.

data_table.Presentation: Acute severe behavioural disturbance, active aggression, refusing oral medication
data_table.Relevant history: Schizophrenia, no known QT prolongation, no recent alcohol or benzodiazepine

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg, with strict avoidance of concurrent parenteral benzodiazepines and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: The NSW Health clinical care standard for acute severe behavioural disturbance identifies IM olanzapine and IM droperidol as first-line options when parenteral rapid tranquillisation is required after failed de-escalation. IM olanzapine 10 mg is a defensible first choice; the specific safety flag is to avoid concurrent parenteral benzodiazepines because of respiratory depression risk. Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring is mandatory (Source: NSW Health ABD clinical care standard; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg with intramuscular promethazine 50 mg, with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and a baseline 12-lead ECG once feasible
options.rationale: The high-dose haloperidol/promethazine cocktail is not preferred in Australian practice; haloperidol has substantial QT and EPS risk and promethazine adds sedation and anticholinergic burden without clear benefit. Would rarely be correct (Source: NSW Health ABD standard).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg as monotherapy, with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and airway equipment ready at the bedside for the next 2 hours
options.rationale: IM midazolam monotherapy carries meaningful risk of respiratory depression, especially at 10 mg, and provides no antipsychotic effect for schizophrenic agitation. Would rarely be correct (Source: NSW Health ABD standard).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Physical restraint alone until behaviour settles, with continuous nursing observation and reassessment for pharmacological therapy after 30 minutes if not settled
options.rationale: Physical restraint without pharmacological adjunct is unsafe, prolongs restraint time, and increases the risk of positional asphyxia and cardiac arrest; restraint is a last resort combined with, not instead of, pharmacological management. (Source: NSW Health ABD standard).
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance
