stem: A 30-year-old primary school teacher attends your GP clinic asking for assessment for possible attention deficit hyperactivity disorder after her nephew was diagnosed. She reports lifelong difficulty finishing tasks, chronic time blindness, poor sleep because her mind races, and multiple career changes. Her school reports at age 8 mention she is bright but does not finish her work. She drives daily including for work, has no seizures, no substance use and is otherwise well. She scores 17/24 on the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Alert, engaging, mild psychomotor restlessness; euthymic; no cognitive deficit at bedside; no dysmorphism
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mIU/L, iron studies within normal limits, FBC and UEC within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence dexamfetamine 5 mg orally twice daily as a therapeutic trial and review clinical response in 4 weeks in general practice before deciding on formal specialist referral for the ADHD assessment
options.rationale: GPs cannot legally initiate stimulants for ADHD in most AU jurisdictions; assessment and initiation are a specialist role in state authority framework.

options.text: Reassure that the ASRS is only a screening tool with limited specificity, provide sleep hygiene advice and refer for CBT for adult inattention symptoms while deferring any formal diagnostic assessment for 6 months
options.rationale: ASRS positive plus functional impairment and lifelong symptoms warrants specialist assessment; deferring 6 months without addressing established impairment is not the AU pathway.
source_refs: RANZCP Adult ADHD clinical practice guideline

options.text: Advise her to stop driving immediately pending diagnostic assessment and treatment initiation as untreated adult ADHD is deemed to preclude a safe class C car licence under Austroads standards
options.rationale: AU Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive does not automatically preclude driving for untreated ADHD; a fitness assessment applies only where symptoms create demonstrated risk.

options.text: Order neuropsychological testing including Wisconsin Card Sort and Trail Making tests in general practice to formally diagnose ADHD before making any specialist referral or considering any treatment options
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing supplements clinical diagnosis but is not the diagnostic gateway; specialist psychiatric interview with collateral history is the primary AU standard.

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist or specialist paediatric-adult ADHD service for structured diagnostic assessment including collateral childhood history, comorbidity screen and consideration of stimulant treatment
options.rationale: AU RANZCP practice guideline requires specialist psychiatrist assessment (or dual-trained paediatrician) for adult ADHD diagnosis including collateral history and comorbidity screen before stimulants are initiated.
source_refs: RANZCP Adult ADHD clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: AU adult ADHD assessment requires specialist psychiatrist review with a structured diagnostic interview, collateral childhood history (school reports, family members), functional impairment across two settings, comorbidity screen and exclusion of alternative causes. Stimulant treatment is initiated by an authorised specialist under state authority. Driving is generally permitted unless active impairment is demonstrated; patients on stimulants should be counselled to declare medications on licence review as per Austroads standards.
key_points: Adult ADHD diagnosis is specialist psychiatrist (or dual paediatrician) responsibility
Collateral childhood history required for diagnosis
Stimulant initiation requires state authority
Driving allowed unless demonstrated impairment (Austroads)
explanation.pearls: Untreated adult ADHD is associated with increased motor vehicle crash risk in cohort studies; stimulant treatment reduces this risk, so document a clear pre and post treatment driving history and encourage patients to consider medication effect on driving performance when planning long or high-risk driving.

sources.label: RANZCP Adult ADHD clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Delusional disorder discrimination
stem: A 52-year-old woman is referred to your community mental health team by her GP because for 18 months she has been convinced her neighbour is releasing carbon monoxide gas through her bedroom wall to poison her. She has had the vents boarded up and installed multiple detectors that consistently read zero. She works full-time as a bookkeeper without difficulty, maintains social contact with three long-term friends, and reports no hallucinations. Her mood is euthymic. On mental state she is well-groomed, articulate and no formal thought disorder. Cognitive screen is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well-groomed, articulate; euthymic; no formal thought disorder; single persistent non-bizarre delusion regarding neighbour poisoning; no hallucinations; insight absent regarding delusion, preserved regarding functioning; MMSE 30/30
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.4 mIU/L, B12 320 pmol/L, folate within normal limits, CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and initial pharmacological approach?

options.text: Schizophrenia paranoid subtype; olanzapine 10 mg orally at night with community mental health team weekly follow-up, weight and metabolic monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks and 3 months
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires 6 months of prodromal or active phase symptoms including hallucinations, negative symptoms or disorganisation; preserved functioning and single non-bizarre delusion fits delusional disorder.

options.text: Late-onset psychosis secondary to dementia; commence donepezil 5 mg orally daily and refer to memory clinic for MRI, formal neuropsychology and progressive cognitive care planning for the household
options.rationale: Normal cognitive screen and preserved functioning make dementia unlikely; donepezil does not treat isolated delusional disorder.

options.text: Delusional disorder (persecutory type); slow low-dose risperidone 0.5 mg orally at night titrated over 6 weeks with regular RANZCP outcome measure review and engagement in trust-building therapy
options.rationale: A single non-bizarre delusion for over one month with preserved functioning, no hallucinations and no thought disorder meets DSM-5-TR delusional disorder criteria; low-dose antipsychotic with slow titration and therapeutic engagement is standard.

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder; monitor without antipsychotic for 4 weeks awaiting spontaneous resolution, review in 4 weeks with the community mental health team before any pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder is under 1 month duration; 18 months excludes this diagnosis.

options.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features; sertraline 100 mg orally daily plus low-dose olanzapine 5 mg orally at night as combination pharmacotherapy for mood-congruent psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: Depressive psychosis requires prominent mood symptoms; she is euthymic and there is no depressive syndrome.

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is diagnosed when a persistent non-bizarre delusion (persecutory, jealous, erotomanic, grandiose or somatic) is present for at least one month, functioning is not markedly impaired outside the delusion, no hallucinations are prominent, and criteria for schizophrenia are not met. Treatment is low-dose antipsychotic (risperidone or olanzapine) with slow titration, plus supportive engagement acknowledging the patient's distress without endorsing the delusion. Insight and treatment adherence are often poor, so slow trust-building is central.
key_points: Delusional disorder = non-bizarre delusion >=1 month, preserved function
No prominent hallucinations, no thought disorder
Low-dose antipsychotic (risperidone) with slow titration
Trust-building engagement without endorsing or challenging delusion directly
explanation.pearls: Response rates in delusional disorder are lower than schizophrenia and require patience with slow titration and long trials; folie a deux (shared delusional disorder) may develop in close contacts who withdraw from the shared belief on separation from the primary case.

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant sequencing
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman in outpatient clinic. She was diagnosed with a first episode of moderate major depressive disorder 14 weeks ago. She commenced sertraline titrated over 6 weeks to 150 mg daily, which she has taken consistently for 8 weeks at the current dose with clear improvement in initiation and appetite but persistent hopelessness, anhedonia and suicidal ideation without plan. PHQ-9 has moved from 20 to 14. Sleep initiation is poor. She tolerates sertraline without side effects, has no active substance use, and completes weekly individual CBT with fidelity. There is no bipolar family history and no manic features. Baseline blood pressure is 118/76.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 42 mcg/L (30-300), vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (>200)
data_table.History: Sertraline 150 mg daily for 8 weeks at target dose, weekly CBT with a psychologist, PHQ-9 20 -> 14 with persistent hopelessness and suicidal ideation, no bipolarity, no substances, no thyroid or cardiac disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose to 200 mg daily and review response at four weeks in clinic
options.rationale: Sertraline shows a flat dose-response above 150 to 200 mg for antidepressant effect, and dose escalation beyond an already therapeutic dose that has been trialled for 8 weeks confers little additional benefit relative to switch or augmentation strategies. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

options.text: Cross-taper sertraline to venlafaxine extended-release and titrate to 225 mg daily over three weeks
options.rationale: After an adequate SSRI trial (at least 4 weeks at target dose) with partial response, RANZCP and STAR-D data support switching to a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor such as venlafaxine. Cross-tapering avoids withdrawal, and titration to 225 mg daily engages noradrenergic mechanism absent with SSRI. Blood pressure monitoring is required as venlafaxine can raise BP dose-dependently. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

options.text: Add fluoxetine 20 mg daily to the current sertraline regimen as combination antidepressant therapy
options.rationale: Combining two SSRIs offers no additional benefit and substantially increases the risk of serotonin syndrome, particularly with fluoxetine's long half-life. This is contraindicated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Add tranylcypromine 10 mg daily on top of the current sertraline for augmentation of antidepressant effect
options.rationale: Combining an SSRI with a non-selective irreversible MAOI is contraindicated because of catastrophic serotonin syndrome risk. A washout of 5 to 6 weeks after fluoxetine or 2 weeks after most other SSRIs is required before starting an MAOI. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: MAOIs)

options.text: Cease sertraline abruptly and start amitriptyline 25 mg nightly the next day for treatment-resistant depression
options.rationale: Abrupt SSRI cessation risks discontinuation syndrome, and starting a TCA without cross-taper and without addressing suicidality with a monitoring plan is unsafe. Amitriptyline is also more lethal in overdose than SSRIs or SNRIs. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

explanation.summary: After a partial response to an adequate SSRI trial, RANZCP guidance and STAR-D data support either switching to another class such as an SNRI, or augmenting with lithium, second-generation antipsychotic, or a psychological therapy. Venlafaxine XR to 225 mg engages noradrenergic mechanism absent from SSRIs. Blood pressure and adherence are monitored during titration.
key_points: Adequate SSRI trial = target dose for at least 4 weeks; here 8 weeks at 150 mg satisfies
Partial response at adequate SSRI trial -> switch class (SNRI, mirtazapine) or augment (lithium, quetiapine, aripiprazole)
Venlafaxine XR requires BP monitoring; target 225 mg for treatment-resistant depression
SSRI + MAOI and SSRI + SSRI combinations are contraindicated (serotonin syndrome)
explanation.pearls: Cross-taper duration for sertraline to venlafaxine is typically 2 weeks: reduce sertraline by 50 mg per week while introducing venlafaxine 37.5 mg then increasing weekly.

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal management
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 48-year-old man for elective alcohol detoxification. He has been drinking 20 standard drinks per day for 8 years. His last drink was 14 hours ago. He has a history of tonic-clonic seizure during a prior unassisted withdrawal 3 years ago but no delirium tremens. He is medically stable, taking no other substances, and has no benzodiazepine tolerance issues. On admission examination he is tremulous with mild diaphoresis, orientated to person, place and time, and following commands. His CIWA-Ar score is currently 12 and rising over the last 2 hours. He weighs 82 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 152/94, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: sodium 140 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), phosphate 0.7 mmol/L (0.75-1.5), LFTs mildly deranged with AST 92 U/L (<35), platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), thiamine and B12 not yet measured
data_table.History: Prior tonic-clonic seizure during unassisted withdrawal, no prior DTs, no other substances, no allergies, weight 82 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Give oral haloperidol 5 mg now and repeat every 4 hours as required for withdrawal-associated agitation
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are not first-line for alcohol withdrawal. They are added only when psychotic features persist despite adequate benzodiazepine loading, not as monotherapy. (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guideline)

options.text: Commence phenytoin 15 mg/kg intravenous loading dose to prevent further alcohol-withdrawal seizures
options.rationale: Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures. Adequate benzodiazepine dosing is the seizure-preventive agent of choice in alcohol withdrawal. (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guideline)

options.text: Give parenteral thiamine 300 mg then symptom-triggered diazepam by CIWA-Ar with a scheduled loading dose
options.rationale: Australian withdrawal guidance is symptom-triggered benzodiazepine (diazepam) titrated to CIWA-Ar with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Prior withdrawal seizure raises baseline risk, so a scheduled front-loading dose of diazepam 20 mg is added on top of the CIWA-Ar protocol. (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guideline)

options.text: Prescribe fixed-dose oral diazepam 5 mg every 6 hours regardless of the current CIWA-Ar score
options.rationale: Fixed low-dose scheduling under-treats moderate withdrawal and is associated with higher seizure rates than symptom-triggered dosing. Symptom-triggered dosing tailored to the CIWA-Ar score is the current standard. (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guideline)

options.text: Commence oral naltrexone 50 mg daily now and continue CIWA-Ar assessment every 4 hours through withdrawal
options.rationale: Naltrexone is a relapse-prevention agent commenced after withdrawal is complete, not during acute withdrawal. It has no role in symptom control during the acute withdrawal period. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Use Disorder)

explanation.summary: Australian alcohol withdrawal guidance uses symptom-triggered diazepam titrated to a validated withdrawal scale (CIWA-Ar) as the cornerstone. Parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV or IM is given before any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy in this population. A prior withdrawal seizure is a clear indication for a scheduled loading dose of diazepam in addition to CIWA-driven dosing. Electrolyte replacement (magnesium, phosphate, potassium) is performed early.
key_points: Symptom-triggered diazepam via CIWA-Ar is first-line for moderate to severe withdrawal
Thiamine 300 mg IV/IM before any glucose infusion in AUD to prevent Wernicke
Prior withdrawal seizure warrants scheduled loading dose (e.g. diazepam 20 mg) in addition to symptom-triggered protocol
Replace magnesium, phosphate, potassium; monitor for arrhythmia risk
explanation.pearls: Wernicke prophylaxis is 300 mg IV/IM thiamine daily for 3 days; a Wernicke-suspected patient requires 500 mg IV three times daily for 2-3 days.

subtopic_detail: Clozapine dosing when a patient stops smoking
stem: A 38-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for four years and smokes 30 cigarettes daily. He is admitted to a smoke-free ward, stops smoking abruptly and accepts nicotine patches.

data_table.Observations: BP 104/68 lying, HR 104, afebrile, full blood count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reduce the clozapine dose and take a clozapine plasma level today
options.rationale: Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2; stopping smoking removes the induction and clozapine concentrations rise substantially within days, producing sedation, hypersalivation and seizure risk. Dose reduction guided by plasma levels is the correct response. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

options.text: Withhold clozapine for 48 hours and repeat the full blood count
options.rationale: Withholding with urgent haematology review is right for suspected neutropenia or myocarditis. His count is normal, and a 48-hour break risks needing retitration from a low dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the current dose and add benztropine for the hypersalivation
options.rationale: An anticholinergic can be used for isolated clozapine-induced hypersalivation in a patient at a stable therapeutic level. Here it treats one symptom of rising toxicity and adds delirium risk. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

options.text: Remove the nicotine patch, since it raises the clozapine level
options.rationale: Removing replacement is appropriate for a local skin reaction only. Nicotine does not induce CYP1A2; the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke do, so the patch is not the problem. (Source: AMH: Nicotine)

options.text: Increase the clozapine dose to cover the stress of admission
options.rationale: An increase is considered for breakthrough psychotic symptoms at a subtherapeutic level. His signs are of excess, not relapse, and an increase could precipitate seizures. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

explanation.summary: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke, not nicotine, induce CYP1A2, the main enzyme clearing clozapine and olanzapine. Abrupt cessation removes that induction over a few days and clozapine concentrations can rise by half or more, producing sedation, hypersalivation, postural hypotension, tachycardia, confusion and seizures. Anticipatory dose reduction with plasma level monitoring is indicated whenever a smoker on clozapine stops or is admitted to a smoke-free facility, and the reverse problem arises on discharge when smoking resumes and levels fall. The same induction affects olanzapine and theophylline; because the interaction is caused by smoke rather than nicotine, nicotine replacement can and should be continued.
key_points: Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2; nicotine replacement does not
Clozapine and olanzapine levels rise after smoking cessation, often within days
Reduce the dose and monitor plasma levels when a smoker on clozapine stops
Levels fall again if the patient resumes smoking after discharge
explanation.pearls: Rising clozapine levels present as sedation, hypersalivation and postural drop before they present as a seizure, which is why a level is taken on the first day of these symptoms rather than after an event.

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar called by the postnatal ward at 02:00. A 32-year-old primipara is 9 days postnatal after a normal vaginal delivery. Over the last 48 hours she has been increasingly agitated, sleeping less than 2 hours per night, speaking pressured and rapidly about needing to protect the baby from spiritual harm, and today insisted the baby is possessed and requires cleansing rituals. She has personal history of bipolar I disorder untreated in pregnancy following her decision to stop lithium 3 years ago when planning conception. Her mother had a psychiatric admission after her own second child was born. On assessment tonight she is disorientated to date, has fluctuating attention, and told the midwife earlier that she saw shadows moving around the baby's cot. Baby is currently with her partner in the ward.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 112, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, TSH 1.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes and calcium within normal limits, urinalysis clear, no illicit substance use, CT head deferred pending medical review
data_table.History: 9 days postpartum, prior bipolar I stopped lithium 3 years ago, maternal aunt puerperal admission, agitation with delusional beliefs about baby, hallucinations reported, sleep <2 h nightly for 48 h

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Discharge overnight with the partner as informal supervision and outpatient perinatal team follow-up in 48 hours
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with elevated risk of maternal suicide and infanticide. Discharge home is unsafe even with informal partner supervision. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

options.text: Prescribe oral zopiclone 7.5 mg nightly to normalise sleep and review the ward assessment during daytime rounds
options.rationale: A sedative-hypnotic alone will not address the psychotic illness, offers no antipsychotic effect, and leaves the mother and baby at ongoing risk. Sleep is important but is a consequence not the driver of the emergency. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

options.text: Remove the baby from the ward tonight and commence sertraline 50 mg for postpartum depression with psychotic features
options.rationale: This is postpartum psychosis, not postpartum depression, and starting an SSRI alone is inadequate. Bipolar-spectrum postpartum psychosis is typically managed with lithium and an atypical antipsychotic, not SSRI monotherapy. Baby separation is a decision made in collaboration with the mother-baby unit and child protection colleagues, not unilaterally at the outset. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

options.text: Admit to a mother-baby psychiatric unit under mental health legislation and start olanzapine with perinatal plan
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis (delusions about the baby, disorientation, hallucinations, sleep disturbance) with prior bipolar I disorder and a family history of puerperal psychosis carries very high risk of maternal suicide and infanticide. Admission to a mother-baby psychiatric unit under mental health legislation with continuous observation, commencement of an atypical antipsychotic acutely, and specialist perinatal assessment to reinstate lithium (weighing feeding decisions) is the RANZCP-endorsed pathway. Baby remains with mother in supervised MBU setting where clinically safe. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

options.text: Give intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg and physical restraint pending transfer to a general adult psychiatric unit
options.rationale: Non-emergency use of physical restraint and high-dose typical antipsychotic monotherapy is not the first step; oral atypical antipsychotic is preferred where the patient can accept oral medication. Transfer to a general adult unit rather than a mother-baby unit fragments care and separates baby from mother without clear necessity. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency, typically onset within the first 2 weeks, with delusions (often about the baby), sleep disturbance, agitation and disorientation. Bipolar I history and family history of puerperal psychosis substantially raise risk. Management requires urgent admission to a mother-baby psychiatric unit where possible, mental health legislation involvement, atypical antipsychotic and specialist perinatal review for lithium reinstatement.
key_points: Postpartum psychosis: onset <2 weeks postpartum with delusions, hallucinations, disorientation, sleep loss
Prior bipolar I and family history of puerperal psychosis carry >30% recurrence risk
MBU admission preferred; MHA framework used when insight impaired
Lithium is highly effective but excreted in breast milk; specialist decision on feeding
explanation.pearls: Puerperal psychosis with bipolar I background has a 30-50% recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancies; antenatal lithium prophylaxis after obstetric-psychiatric consultation reduces recurrence.

sources.label: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

subtopic_detail: Cannabis-induced vs primary psychosis
stem: You are the mental health registrar reviewing a 20-year-old male university student in a community psychiatric emergency clinic. Over the past 6 weeks he has developed persecutory delusions about being tracked by a coordinated group, auditory hallucinations of two voices commenting on his behaviour, and social withdrawal. Onset was gradual over 4 weeks; the last 2 weeks his function has collapsed. He commenced daily high-potency cannabis (~1.5 g/day of a THC-dominant product) 12 months ago and stopped completely 3 weeks ago on family insistence. There is no other substance use, no alcohol above two standard drinks per week, no synthetic cannabinoid use, no prescribed medications, no head injury, no seizure history. There is a family history of schizophrenia in a maternal uncle. Mental state examination confirms first-rank symptoms with preserved orientation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, TSH 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes and calcium within normal limits, LFTs normal, urine drug screen positive for cannabinoids (from prior use, up to 30 days), negative for methamphetamine and cocaine, CT head normal
data_table.History: 6 weeks psychotic symptoms, cannabis daily 12 months then stopped 3 weeks ago, no other substances, family history schizophrenia (maternal uncle), function collapsed over 2 weeks

lead_in: How would you formulate this presentation and what is the most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Diagnose cannabis-induced psychotic disorder likely to resolve within 24 hours and observe without any antipsychotic
options.rationale: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder typically resolves within 1 month of abstinence in true cases. This patient has been abstinent for 3 weeks with persistent worsening symptoms and 2 weeks of collapsed function, suggesting a primary psychotic disorder or cannabis has unmasked a primary process. Observation without treatment is unsafe. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

options.text: Commence lorazepam 1 mg twice daily as required and defer antipsychotic while awaiting spontaneous resolution over weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy has no antipsychotic activity and does not address the underlying illness. Delaying antipsychotic prolongs untreated psychosis, which is associated with worse long-term functional outcome. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily as first-line therapy for likely major depression with psychotic features
options.rationale: The presentation is a primary psychotic disorder (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, 6 weeks duration, collapsed function) rather than depression with psychotic features. Mood symptoms are secondary and an SSRI alone is inadequate. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

options.text: Commence quetiapine 100 mg titrated to 400 mg over 4 weeks as first-line therapy for likely bipolar depression
options.rationale: There is no history of mood episodes, no elevated or depressed mood, and no relevant family history of bipolar disorder here. Diagnosing bipolar disorder without any mood evidence is unsupported. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

options.text: Commence risperidone titrated to 2 to 4 mg, refer to early psychosis intervention, and provide cannabis relapse plan
options.rationale: Persistent psychotic symptoms 3 weeks after cannabis cessation with 6 weeks total duration, collapsed function and a family history of schizophrenia meet criteria for a schizophrenia-spectrum first episode psychosis. Cannabis is best formulated as a precipitating rather than sole cause. RANZCP and Australian EPPIC guidance is early antipsychotic (low-dose atypical such as risperidone or olanzapine), early intervention service referral, psychoeducation about cannabis as a relapse and severity driver, and safety planning. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder typically resolves within 4 weeks of abstinence. Persistent psychotic symptoms 3 weeks after cessation with collapsed function and family history of schizophrenia are more consistent with a schizophrenia-spectrum first episode of psychosis, with cannabis as a precipitating factor. Australian EPPIC guidance is early antipsychotic (low dose), early psychosis intervention team referral, psychoeducation and safety planning.
key_points: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder should resolve within ~4 weeks of abstinence
Persistent symptoms beyond that = re-diagnose as primary psychotic disorder (cannabis precipitant)
First-episode psychosis pharmacotherapy: low-dose atypical (risperidone 1-4 mg, olanzapine 5-10 mg)
Cannabis use increases lifetime schizophrenia risk 2-4 fold; high-potency THC increases it further
explanation.pearls: Cannabis-related psychotic conversion to schizophrenia occurs in ~34% of cannabis-induced psychosis cases at 8-year follow-up (Danish register data 2018).

subtopic_detail: Autism spectrum disorder in adult women
stem: You are the general practice registrar in an adult clinic. A 28-year-old professional woman presents with 12 months of severe fatigue and burnout following a workplace restructure. She reports lifelong difficulty with sustained group social interaction, exhaustion after work social events, intense special interests (medieval history, and prior periods of hyper-focused folklore research), sensory sensitivities to fluorescent light and clothing labels, and a longstanding sense of masking to fit in socially. She has previously been diagnosed with anxiety and depression at ages 16 and 22 with only partial response to sertraline and CBT. She has close but limited friendships with women who share her special interests. Her general practitioner is considering a formal neurodevelopmental assessment. She is not autistic-identifying at this time. She has no psychotic features, no substance use, and no mood elevation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 74, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 62 mcg/L (30-300), vitamin D 68 nmol/L (>50), TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes and glucose within normal limits, PHQ-9 12 (mild-moderate), GAD-7 14 (moderate), AUDIT 3, PDSS-SR 6
data_table.History: 12 months burnout, lifelong social difficulty, intense special interests, sensory sensitivities, masking; prior anxiety and depression diagnoses partially responsive to sertraline and CBT; no psychosis, no substances, no mood elevation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in your assessment plan?

options.text: Refer for structured autism assessment with ADOS-2 and ADI-R and continue psychological therapy for anxiety in parallel
options.rationale: The presentation (lifelong social exhaustion, intense special interests, sensory sensitivities, masking, and partial response to standard anxiety and depression care with recurrent burnout) is characteristic of previously-undiagnosed autism spectrum disorder in an adult woman. Australian adult ASD guidance (RANZCP and the Australian National Guideline for Assessment) supports structured assessment with clinicians experienced in the female phenotype, using ADOS-2 and ADI-R alongside a developmental history from a childhood informant. Concurrent management of comorbid anxiety and burnout continues in parallel. (Source: Australian ASD Diagnostic Guideline)

options.text: Reassure her this is generalised anxiety disorder and increase sertraline to the maximum dose of 200 mg daily
options.rationale: The clinical picture is far broader than an anxiety disorder alone. Increasing sertraline to maximum without addressing the underlying neurodevelopmental profile misses the primary diagnostic question and repeats prior partial-response cycles. (Source: RANZCP ADHD/ASD adult resources)

options.text: Perform brief AQ-10 screening and, if score under 6, discharge from any further adult neurodevelopmental workup
options.rationale: The AQ-10 is a screen with moderate sensitivity; a low score should not exclude ASD when the clinical picture is strongly suggestive, and it is known to underdetect the female phenotype. Structured assessment remains warranted. (Source: Australian ASD Diagnostic Guideline)

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate 10 mg daily for suspected adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder empirically
options.rationale: Empirically starting stimulant medication without a diagnostic assessment for ADHD is not appropriate. In addition, the presentation here fits ASD better than adult ADHD, though the two can co-occur; formal assessment first is essential. (Source: RANZCP ADHD/ASD adult resources)

options.text: Refer for inpatient adult psychiatric admission today for stabilisation of burnout and multi-system fatigue symptoms
options.rationale: There is no risk to self or others, no severe functional collapse requiring inpatient care, and no psychotic or manic features. Outpatient assessment and support is appropriate. (Source: RANZCP ADHD/ASD adult resources)

explanation.summary: Undiagnosed adult female ASD often presents in the general practice or adult psychiatry clinic as recurrent burnout, partial response to standard depression and anxiety care, and lifelong social masking with sensory sensitivities and intense circumscribed interests. Structured assessment with clinicians experienced in the female phenotype, using ADOS-2 and ADI-R with childhood informant history, is the standard in Australia. Concurrent management of comorbid anxiety and depression continues.
key_points: Female ASD presentation: masking, exhaustion after socialising, intense special interests, sensory sensitivities, partial response to anxiety/depression care
AQ-10 sensitivity is modest, especially in the female phenotype; do not use as a rule-out
ADOS-2 + ADI-R + childhood informant history is standard adult diagnostic assessment
Comorbid anxiety, depression, ADHD common; manage in parallel
explanation.pearls: Adult women may not receive an ASD diagnosis until their 30s-40s despite lifelong features, because clinician training and screening tools were largely designed on male childhood samples.

subtopic_detail: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to see a 22-year-old woman on the medical ward. She was admitted 3 days ago via emergency after 2 weeks of subacute onset of behavioural change (odd laughter, agitation), paranoid delusions, and orofacial dyskinesias. During today's ward round she had a 90 second focal aware seizure with right facial twitching and afterwards was mute for 20 minutes. Vital signs earlier showed transient tachycardia to 138 and blood pressure fluctuation between 92/58 and 168/98 within 30 minutes. The bedside neurological examination is inconsistent. She has no prior psychiatric or seizure history. She does not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit substances. Screening MRI brain has been reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118 with fluctuation, blood pressure fluctuating 92/58 to 168/98, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: full blood count within normal limits, urea 5.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 68 micromol/L (60-110), C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (<5), TSH within normal limits, HIV and syphilis serology negative, urine drug screen negative, MRI brain normal, EEG shows generalised slowing with extreme delta brush pattern intermittently, CSF pleocytosis 42 white cells/microL with lymphocyte predominance and elevated CSF protein 0.68 g/L (<0.45), CSF glucose within normal limits, oligoclonal bands positive
data_table.History: 2 weeks subacute behavioural change, dyskinesias, focal seizure today, autonomic instability, no substances, no prior psychiatric or neurological history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg orally daily for suspected first-episode psychosis and defer further neurological workup
options.rationale: The pentad of subacute behavioural change, orofacial dyskinesias, focal seizure, autonomic instability, and characteristic EEG (extreme delta brush) with CSF pleocytosis is highly suggestive of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Antipsychotic monotherapy without further workup will not treat the underlying process and antipsychotics may worsen catatonic and NMS-like features. (Source: RANZCP Autoimmune Encephalitis)

options.text: Send CSF and serum for anti-NMDA antibody, image pelvis for teratoma, and start empirical first-line immunotherapy
options.rationale: The clinical picture is classic anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: female patient in her early 20s with subacute psychiatric symptoms, dyskinesias, seizures, autonomic instability, and characteristic EEG (extreme delta brush) with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein. In young women, ovarian teratoma is present in over 50% and its removal is part of definitive treatment. Australian and international neurology guidance is to send CSF and serum for anti-NMDA IgG, image for tumour, and commence first-line immunotherapy (steroids plus IVIG or plasma exchange) empirically pending antibody confirmation because early treatment improves outcomes. (Source: RANZCP Autoimmune Encephalitis)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for likely conversion disorder and refer to outpatient psychiatry follow-up
options.rationale: Conversion disorder is a diagnosis of exclusion and cannot account for CSF pleocytosis, an abnormal EEG with extreme delta brush, autonomic instability and focal seizure. Missing autoimmune encephalitis has serious consequences. (Source: RANZCP Autoimmune Encephalitis)

options.text: Load with sodium valproate 20 mg/kg intravenously and monitor for further seizures without further diagnostic workup
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in a 22-year-old woman of reproductive age without a proven epilepsy diagnosis and without pregnancy prevention counselling. It also does not address the underlying autoimmune process. (Source: RANZCP Autoimmune Encephalitis)

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy given the presence of catatonic features and prominent orofacial dyskinesias
options.rationale: ECT may have a role in refractory catatonia in autoimmune encephalitis but is not the initial step; immunotherapy plus tumour search is the priority. Using ECT without addressing the underlying autoimmune process is inappropriate. (Source: RANZCP Autoimmune Encephalitis)

explanation.summary: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis presents with a characteristic pentad of subacute behavioural change, dyskinesias, seizures, autonomic instability and dysphasic mutism, most commonly in young women. Extreme delta brush on EEG is highly specific and CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein. In women under 45, ovarian teratoma is present in more than half of cases and its removal is part of definitive treatment. First-line immunotherapy (methylprednisolone plus IVIG or plasma exchange) is started empirically pending antibody confirmation. Rituximab and cyclophosphamide are second-line for refractory disease.
key_points: Pentad: behavioural change, dyskinesias, seizures, autonomic instability, dysphasic mutism
EEG extreme delta brush is highly specific
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis + elevated protein + positive oligoclonal bands; anti-NMDA antibody in serum + CSF (CSF more sensitive)
Ovarian teratoma in >50% of women <45; removal is part of definitive treatment
explanation.pearls: Anti-NMDA CSF antibody sensitivity ~100% vs ~85% in serum; testing both increases yield. Rituximab is added when there is no response to first-line therapy within 2 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Treatment-refractory schizophrenia after clozapine myocarditis
stem: You are the senior psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old man with schizophrenia. He has failed adequate trials (>=6 weeks at target dose) of risperidone 6 mg, olanzapine 20 mg and paliperidone 12 mg. Two years ago clozapine was commenced but ceased at week 3 for probable clozapine-induced myocarditis (troponin rise to 220 ng/L, CRP 82 mg/L, echocardiogram showed globally reduced LV function with EF 42%, no other cause identified). He was rehospitalised. Over the past 2 years he has been on aripiprazole 30 mg plus lurasidone 120 mg with persistent auditory hallucinations, negative symptoms and social withdrawal. Most recent echocardiogram (this week) shows LV EF 60% with no wall motion abnormality. He has been abstinent from all recreational substances for 12 months. Cardiology has been consulted.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count with neutrophils 4.8 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), troponin 6 ng/L (<15), NT-proBNP 62 pg/mL (<125), echocardiogram LV EF 60% with no wall motion abnormality and no diastolic dysfunction, ECG sinus rhythm QTc 420 ms
data_table.History: Schizophrenia with failure of 3 adequate atypical trials, clozapine ceased for myocarditis 2 years ago, current medications aripiprazole + lurasidone with persistent positive and negative symptoms, cardiology reviewed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for symptom control?

options.text: Refer for maintenance bilateral electroconvulsive therapy three times weekly indefinitely as ongoing symptom control
options.rationale: Maintenance ECT is used selectively when medication cannot achieve adequate response, but it does not replace an antipsychotic trial that could still deliver superior outcome. Clozapine remains the strongest evidence-based agent for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and should be re-considered before indefinite ECT is chosen. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Add high-dose quetiapine 800 mg nightly to the current aripiprazole plus lurasidone regimen and continue indefinitely
options.rationale: Polypharmacy with three atypical antipsychotics has no evidence base, substantially increases metabolic, cardiac (QT prolongation) and anticholinergic burden, and does not achieve the response rate of a clozapine trial in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Undertake supervised clozapine re-challenge with slower titration and structured cardiac surveillance with cardiology
options.rationale: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of 2 or more adequate trials at target dose) is the specific indication for clozapine. Prior clozapine-induced myocarditis is a relative not absolute contraindication; Australian case series describe successful re-challenge in about half of selected patients using slower titration and structured cardiac surveillance in collaboration with cardiology. Current cardiac status (normal EF, normal troponin, no ongoing cardiac abnormality) supports a considered re-challenge with informed consent. Clinical guidelines require weekly troponin and CRP for at least the first 4 weeks with prompt cessation on rise. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Discontinue all antipsychotic medication and manage with high-dose lorazepam 4 mg four times daily for symptom control
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy is not an evidence-based treatment for schizophrenia and increases risks of dependence, sedation and respiratory depression. It offers no antipsychotic activity. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Add long-acting paliperidone 150 mg intramuscular injection monthly to the current oral aripiprazole and lurasidone
options.rationale: The patient has already failed adequate trials of paliperidone (12 mg oral, equivalent to LAI). Repeating an ineffective agent does not resolve treatment resistance and adds side-effect burden. Clozapine trial is the evidence-based next step. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials) is treated with clozapine. Prior clozapine-induced myocarditis is a relative rather than absolute contraindication; supervised re-challenge with slower titration and structured cardiac surveillance in collaboration with cardiology has been successful in approximately half of published Australian cases. Polypharmacy with additional atypical antipsychotics has no evidence base and increases metabolic and cardiac burden.
key_points: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia = failure of >=2 adequate trials of different antipsychotics at target dose
Clozapine is the definitive agent; re-challenge after prior myocarditis is possible in selected patients with cardiology co-management
Slower clozapine titration + weekly troponin and CRP for 4 weeks; stop and refer immediately on any rise
Baseline and follow-up echocardiogram; ECG at baseline, week 2, week 4
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced myocarditis usually occurs in the first 4 weeks; a slower titration (25 mg every 3-4 days initially) plus vigilant surveillance halves incidence of severe cases in Australian re-challenge protocols.

subtopic_detail: Lithium initiation baseline workup
stem: You are the community psychiatry registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman with confirmed bipolar I disorder, currently euthymic 4 weeks after a hypomanic episode. She has had two clear manic episodes and one depressive episode in the past 3 years. The consultant recommends starting lithium for maintenance. She has no significant medical history, is not pregnant (LMP 1 week ago, using condoms consistently), is a non-smoker, and drinks 4 standard drinks weekly. She takes no regular medications and has no known allergies. She wants to complete her studies and eventually plan a pregnancy in 2 to 3 years.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.History: Bipolar I, 2 manic + 1 depressive episodes over 3 years, currently euthymic, LMP 1 week ago, no meds, no comorbidities

lead_in: Which baseline investigation set is most appropriate before starting lithium?

options.text: Full blood count, C-reactive protein, HbA1c, and vitamin B12 only; no imaging or ECG required before initiation
options.rationale: This omits renal function, TFTs, calcium, ECG and pregnancy test which are the specific relevant tests for lithium. Adding non-specific tests instead misses the target organs affected by lithium. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Urea, creatinine, electrolytes, thyroid function, calcium, ECG, pregnancy test, and weight recorded today
options.rationale: Standard pre-lithium workup includes renal function (baseline for later comparison), TFTs (lithium causes hypothyroidism in 20 percent), calcium (hyperparathyroidism association), ECG in patients with cardiac risk or age >40 (also for baseline QT), pregnancy test (lithium is teratogenic; Ebstein anomaly signal), and weight. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: MRI brain and EEG to rule out structural or epileptic conditions before beginning any mood stabiliser treatment
options.rationale: MRI and EEG are not routine pre-lithium workup; they are reserved for atypical clinical features or first-episode workup where organic disease is suspected. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: 24-hour urine collection for creatinine clearance and iothalamate GFR before every mood stabiliser starts today
options.rationale: 24-hour collection and iothalamate GFR are not routine baseline tests. Serum creatinine with eGFR is standard; more detailed renal testing is reserved for suspected chronic kidney disease. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Fasting lipids, iron studies, HbA1c, and echocardiogram are all required baseline tests before starting lithium
options.rationale: Lipids, iron and HbA1c are relevant for antipsychotic metabolic monitoring, not lithium. Echocardiogram is not routine unless cardiac disease is suspected. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

explanation.summary: Pre-lithium baseline workup targets the organs lithium affects: renal function (UEC and eGFR), thyroid function (hypothyroidism in 20 percent), calcium (hyperparathyroidism), ECG if age >40 or cardiac risk, pregnancy test (Ebstein anomaly and other teratogenicity), and weight. During treatment lithium levels are checked 5 to 7 days after each dose change and every 3 months once stable, with UEC/TFTs/calcium every 6 months. Trough level target is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance; 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L for acute mania.
key_points: Baseline: UEC, TFTs, calcium, ECG (age >40 or cardiac risk), pregnancy test, weight
Ongoing: lithium level 12 hours post-dose, every 3 months once stable
UEC, TFTs, calcium every 6 months during maintenance
Maintenance target 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L; acute mania 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: Lithium clearance falls approximately 15 percent for every 10-year age increase after 40 and rises 30 to 50 percent in pregnancy (dose usually increased in T2/T3, halved immediately before delivery); check level within 12 hours of birth.

subtopic_detail: Initial organic screen
stem: You are the ED registrar assessing a 19-year-old university student brought in by parents with a 3 week history of paranoid delusions (belief he is being tracked), auditory hallucinations, and social withdrawal. He denies substance use but parents suspect cannabis. He has no fever, no headache, no neurological symptoms, no seizures, and no recent travel. He is on no medications and has no personal or family history of psychiatric illness. He appears clinically well hydrated and oriented. Physical and neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.MSE: Thought-disordered, paranoid delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, blunted affect, cognition intact
data_table.Neuro: GCS 15, cranial nerves intact, no focal deficits, no meningism, no movement abnormalities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation set?

options.text: MRI brain with contrast and lumbar puncture for CSF anti-NMDA antibodies on every first episode of psychosis case
options.rationale: MRI and LP are indicated when features suggest anti-NMDA encephalitis (movement disorder, seizures, autonomic instability, rapid cognitive decline) or other structural or inflammatory disease, not routinely on all FEP. (Source: RANZCP Psychosis)

options.text: 24-hour urinary catecholamines and metanephrines to rule out phaeochromocytoma-related psychiatric manifestations
options.rationale: Phaeochromocytoma presents with paroxysmal hypertension, headaches, palpitations and sweating rather than psychotic symptoms. This is not routine FEP workup. (Source: RANZCP Psychosis)

options.text: FBC, UEC, LFTs, CRP, TFTs, B12/folate, urine drug screen, hCG if appropriate, and CT brain if focal signs
options.rationale: First-episode psychosis workup screens for organic causes: metabolic (UEC, calcium, LFTs, TSH, B12/folate), infection (FBC, CRP), substances (UDS), and structural pathology (CT/MRI only if focal signs, atypical features, or age extremes). Routine MRI/EEG on all FEP is not evidence based but is common practice; national guidance requires imaging when clinically indicated. (Source: RANZCP Psychosis)

options.text: PET scan of the brain to characterise dopamine receptor availability before commencing any antipsychotic therapy
options.rationale: Dopamine PET is a research tool; it does not guide antipsychotic choice or diagnosis in routine clinical care. (Source: RANZCP Psychosis)

options.text: Full lupus autoantibody panel including ANA, dsDNA, ENA, complement, ANCA at the first ED assessment routinely
options.rationale: Autoimmune workup is targeted to clinical features suggesting cerebral lupus or vasculitis (skin, joints, rash, renal signs), not routine for all FEP presentations. (Source: RANZCP Psychosis)

explanation.summary: First-episode psychosis workup screens targeted organic causes: metabolic (UEC, calcium, LFTs, TSH, B12/folate), infection (FBC, CRP), substances (urine drug screen), and structural (CT/MRI when focal signs, atypical features, or first psychosis in older adults). Neuroimaging is not universally required in young patients with a typical presentation, but is commonly done. Anti-NMDA encephalitis is considered when there is a movement disorder, seizure, autonomic dysfunction, or rapid cognitive decline. Early referral to an early psychosis service and offer of low-dose second-generation antipsychotic are core actions.
key_points: Screen: UEC, LFTs, calcium, TFTs, B12/folate, FBC, CRP, urine drug screen, glucose
Neuroimaging: focal signs, atypical features, first psychosis after age 40
Consider anti-NMDA encephalitis if movement, autonomic, seizure features
Refer to early psychosis intervention service
explanation.pearls: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis triggers include ovarian teratoma (young women 60 percent) and herpes simplex virus infection; screening pelvic ultrasound is indicated when this is suspected.

subtopic_detail: Acute mania first-line pharmacotherapy
stem: You are the psychiatric registrar admitting a 28-year-old man with 6 days of florid mania: elevated mood, grandiose delusions of being a business magnate, 2 hours sleep per night, pressured speech, and disinhibited spending. He has a 2 year history of bipolar I with 3 prior admissions. He is not on any current mood stabiliser (stopped lithium 6 months ago due to weight gain). He has no medical comorbidities, no substance use, and is not planning fatherhood. He is willing to take oral medication.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 98, blood pressure 132/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.MSE: Elevated mood, grandiose delusions, pressured speech, flight of ideas, no active psychotic threat
data_table.Bloods: UEC, LFTs, TSH, calcium all normal; beta hCG not applicable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily titrated to therapeutic dose plus zolpidem 10 mg nocte for sleep for two weeks
options.rationale: SSRIs are contraindicated as monotherapy in acute mania because they can worsen or prolong mania. Antidepressants in bipolar are used only for depression with concurrent mood stabiliser cover. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Carbamazepine 200 mg oral BD titrated with therapeutic drug monitoring plus prazosin 1 mg for sleep at night
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is a second-line agent for mania and requires slow titration; it is not first-line. Prazosin is not indicated. Faster-acting agents are preferred in severe mania. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg TDS as monotherapy for 2 weeks until behavioural containment allows further treatment consideration
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat mania; it manages agitation. A mood stabiliser or antipsychotic is essential to achieve remission. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg oral daily, titrating up over 3 days, with lorazepam 1 to 2 mg TDS for acute agitation and sleep
options.rationale: For acute mania, first-line monotherapy options include lithium, sodium valproate, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, and aripiprazole. Second-generation antipsychotics have faster onset than lithium (days vs 1 to 2 weeks) and are preferred in severe presentations. Adjunct benzodiazepine is standard for acute agitation and sleep. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Electroconvulsive therapy this week as first-line treatment before any trial of pharmacological options is undertaken
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective for mania but is reserved for treatment-resistant cases, severe features (life-threatening exhaustion, catatonia, refusal of intake), or when rapid response is essential and pharmacotherapy has failed or is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for acute mania includes lithium, sodium valproate, or a second-generation antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole, asenapine). Second-generation antipsychotics act faster than lithium (days vs 1 to 2 weeks) and are preferred in severe presentations. Adjunct benzodiazepine (lorazepam 1 to 2 mg TDS PRN) manages agitation and sleep. SSRIs are contraindicated in acute mania. ECT is reserved for severe or refractory cases. Discuss teratogenicity of sodium valproate with reproductive-age patients.
key_points: First-line: lithium, valproate, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole
Second-generation antipsychotics preferred for rapid onset in severe mania
Adjunct lorazepam 1 to 2 mg TDS for agitation and sleep
SSRIs contraindicated; ECT reserved for refractory or severe cases
explanation.pearls: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless a Pregnancy Prevention Program is in place and no alternative exists (TGA and PBS restrictions from 2023 apply).

subtopic_detail: PTSD first-line management
stem: You are the GP seeing a 34-year-old man 4 months after a serious motor vehicle accident. He describes intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance of driving, hypervigilance and irritability. Symptoms are causing occupational impairment. He has no current mood disorder criteria met, no active substance misuse, and no suicidal ideation. He has no significant past psychiatric history and no current medications. He asks how to get better without medication if possible.

data_table.History: MVA 4 months ago, meets DSM-5-TR PTSD criteria, occupational impairment, no comorbid MDD or SUD
data_table.MSE: Anxious mood, congruent affect, no psychotic features, cognition intact, no self-harm
data_table.Function: Off work 3 months, avoiding driving, sleep 4 hours per night

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment recommendation?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily titrated to 100 mg after 2 weeks and continued for at least 12 months as monotherapy
options.rationale: SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) are effective but are second choice to trauma-focused psychotherapy in Australian guidance. They are appropriate when psychotherapy is declined or unavailable, or as adjunct. (Source: Phoenix PTSD)

options.text: Prazosin 1 mg orally nocte, titrated for nightmares, as sole intervention without psychotherapy or SSRI cover
options.rationale: Prazosin is an adjunct for PTSD-related nightmares, not a first-line PTSD treatment. It should be added to trauma-focused psychotherapy or SSRI, not used alone. (Source: Phoenix PTSD)

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg TDS for 6 weeks to reduce hyperarousal symptoms and improve sleep architecture during recovery period
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD; they do not treat core symptoms, worsen dissociation, impair therapy engagement, and cause dependence. (Source: Phoenix PTSD)

options.text: Quetiapine 50 mg nocte for insomnia and low-dose paroxetine for daytime symptoms with weekly follow up review
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line for PTSD; combination pharmacotherapy from the outset is not recommended. Psychotherapy is preferred first with pharmacotherapy considered second line. (Source: Phoenix PTSD)

options.text: Trauma-focused CBT (or EMDR) with weekly sessions over 8 to 12 weeks as first-line evidence-based psychotherapy
options.rationale: The Australian PTSD guidelines (Phoenix Australia) recommend trauma-focused CBT (including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy) or EMDR as first-line treatment, delivered weekly for approximately 8 to 12 sessions. Pharmacotherapy (SSRI/SNRI) is offered when psychotherapy is declined, unavailable, or insufficient. (Source: Phoenix PTSD)

explanation.summary: Trauma-focused psychological therapies (trauma-focused CBT including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy, and EMDR) are first-line evidence-based treatments for adult PTSD, typically weekly for 8 to 12 sessions. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) and the SNRI venlafaxine are effective and used when psychotherapy is declined or unavailable, or as adjunct. Benzodiazepines are not recommended (no efficacy, dependence risk, dissociation). Prazosin can be added for treatment-resistant nightmares.
key_points: First-line: trauma-focused CBT (PE, CPT) or EMDR, 8 to 12 weekly sessions
Pharmacotherapy: SSRI (sertraline, paroxetine) or SNRI (venlafaxine) if psychotherapy declined or insufficient
Avoid benzodiazepines in PTSD
Prazosin adjunct for refractory nightmares only
explanation.pearls: In veterans and refugees with complex PTSD, phased treatment (safety and stabilisation before trauma processing) is emphasised by Phoenix Australia; jumping straight to exposure without stabilisation increases risk of dropout.

subtopic_detail: Benzodiazepine dependence taper
stem: You are the GP seeing a 48-year-old woman on alprazolam 1 mg three times daily for 6 years, initially started for panic disorder. She wants to reduce and eventually stop. She has no current alcohol misuse, no seizure history, and no current mood disorder criteria met. She has partner support and is committed to a slow taper. She has no active plans to conceive and has no other benzodiazepines or z-drugs prescribed. She is otherwise well and on no other regular medications.

data_table.History: Alprazolam 1 mg TDS for 6 years, wants to stop, no alcohol misuse, no seizures, no MDD, supportive partner
data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 122/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.MSE: Anxious but not depressed, no psychosis, no active self-harm, cognition intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management strategy?

options.text: Convert to equivalent diazepam and reduce by 10 percent of the current dose every 2 to 4 weeks with monitoring
options.rationale: The RACGP recommends conversion to equivalent long-acting diazepam (alprazolam 1 mg = diazepam 20 mg approximately, so 3 mg alprazolam ~ 60 mg diazepam) then gradual reduction of 10 percent per 2 to 4 weeks with adjustment based on symptoms. Slower reduction (1 to 2 mg per fortnight) may be needed near the end. Total taper often takes 6 to 12 months. (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence)

options.text: Stop alprazolam abruptly today and prescribe zopiclone 7.5 mg nocte for sleep for 4 weeks then review the taper
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of a high-potency short-acting benzodiazepine after long use risks severe withdrawal including seizures and delirium. Substitution with a z-drug does not prevent withdrawal. (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence)

options.text: Add mirtazapine 30 mg nocte and continue current alprazolam dose indefinitely because it is providing symptomatic relief
options.rationale: Long-term benzodiazepine use for anxiety carries risks (falls, cognitive impairment, dependence, mortality) and is not indicated as chronic treatment. The patient has decided to stop, which is the correct decision. (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence)

options.text: Refer for inpatient detoxification and admission for rapid clonidine-assisted withdrawal over a 7 to 10 day period
options.rationale: Rapid withdrawal is generally not recommended for benzodiazepine dependence; gradual outpatient taper is preferred and safer. Inpatient care is reserved for complex cases or failed outpatient tapers. (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence)

options.text: Prescribe flumazenil infusion in a monitored day-stay unit to accelerate receptor recovery over a 4 to 7 day admission
options.rationale: Flumazenil infusion protocols are not standard care in Australia; risks include seizure and rebound withdrawal. Gradual taper on equivalent diazepam remains the evidence-based approach. (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence)

explanation.summary: Long-term benzodiazepine dependence is managed by conversion to an equivalent dose of long-acting diazepam and gradual reduction of 10 percent per 2 to 4 weeks with symptom-guided pace, often taking 6 to 12 months. Slower steps near the end (0.5 to 1 mg reductions) improve success. Substitute psychological treatment (CBT for panic) and address sleep hygiene. Abrupt cessation risks seizures, delirium, and rebound anxiety. Alprazolam and other high-potency short-acting agents are especially difficult; conversion to diazepam smooths withdrawal.
key_points: Convert to equivalent diazepam (alprazolam 1 mg ~ diazepam 20 mg)
Reduce by 10 percent every 2 to 4 weeks, symptom-guided pace
Total taper typically 6 to 12 months; slower steps near end
Avoid abrupt cessation (seizure, delirium, rebound anxiety)
explanation.pearls: Panic disorder responds to SSRI (sertraline) or SNRI plus CBT; establishing this before or during taper reduces relapse. Alprazolam is on the S8 (controlled) list in Australia; consider TGA and state authority requirements when prescribing long-term.

subtopic_detail: Catatonia recognition and initial management
stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman with a 12-year history of bipolar I disorder on lithium and quetiapine, admitted to the medical ward 3 days ago after her family found her mute in bed. She has stopped eating and drinking, is refusing medication, and has been withdrawn from the community mental health service for two months.

On examination she is awake with eyes open, staring past you, not responsive to questioning. When you raise her right arm above her head it remains suspended for over 60 seconds. She exhibits echopraxia when you touch your nose. When you attempt to move her limb she resists with equal counter-force in both directions. She has been afebrile, saturations normal, blood pressure 128/78, pulse 92. Bloods including CK, TFTs, calcium, and infection screen are normal. Head CT is unremarkable. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score is 18.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: CK 148 U/L (<170), TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), infection screen negative, head CT unremarkable
data_table.Exam: mute, waxy flexibility, echopraxia, gegenhalten, BFCRS 18

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological step?

options.text: Give IM haloperidol 5 mg to sedate her and enable enteral feeding via nasogastric tube for adequate hydration
options.rationale: Haloperidol worsens catatonia and increases risk of NMS; it should be avoided in favour of benzodiazepine trial as the diagnostic and therapeutic step. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Continue current quetiapine and start olanzapine 10 mg for suspected relapse of bipolar affective disorder with psychosis
options.rationale: Antipsychotic monotherapy can worsen catatonia and precipitate malignant catatonia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome; benzodiazepines are first-line, with antipsychotics deferred until catatonia resolves. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Commence electroconvulsive therapy immediately without first trialling any benzodiazepine treatment for this presentation
options.rationale: ECT is second-line after benzodiazepine trial (or first-line in malignant catatonia); a lorazepam challenge is the standard first step in non-malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Give IV lorazepam 2 mg as a challenge and observe for symptomatic response over 5 to 10 minutes
options.rationale: Catatonia (BFCRS 18) is confirmed on positive lorazepam challenge with a benzodiazepine trial; 1 to 2 mg IV lorazepam produces symptomatic relief in 60 to 80 percent of cases within 10 minutes and both diagnoses and initiates ongoing therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Start amantadine 100 mg 12-hourly for NMDA-glutamate modulation as first-line therapy for treatment-refractory catatonia today
options.rationale: Amantadine and NMDA-modulating agents are reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia; the first-line remains benzodiazepine trial before escalation. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome with motor, behavioural, and autonomic features. DSM-5 requires 3 or more of 12 features including catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, stupor, agitation, posturing, mannerisms, stereotypies, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia, and negativism. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale of 3 or more items or 6 or more total suggests catatonia. Lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV or IM) is diagnostic and therapeutic in 60 to 80 percent of cases. Malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, hyperthermia) is a life-threatening variant requiring ECT.
key_points: First-line: lorazepam challenge 1 to 2 mg IV or IM
Continue lorazepam 4 to 8 mg daily divided if responsive
Second-line: ECT (first-line if malignant catatonia)
Avoid antipsychotics until resolved (risk of NMS)
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia clues: fever above 38 C, autonomic instability, elevated CK, rhabdomyolysis; treat as NMS with immediate ECT while withholding antipsychotics. Overlap with NMS is significant; clinical picture often decides.

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome in anorexia nervosa admission
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman referred from the eating disorders clinic. She has a 4-year history of anorexia nervosa (restrictive subtype) and has lost 8 kg over 2 months. Current BMI is 12.8 (weight 34 kg, height 163 cm). She is bradycardic at 42, blood pressure 88/54 lying and 74/48 standing, temperature 35.4, ECG shows sinus bradycardia with corrected QT of 460 ms and prominent U waves.

Admission bloods: sodium 138, potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70 to 1.10), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.50), glucose 3.2 mmol/L, albumin 34 g/L, creatinine 42 umol/L, calcium 2.20 mmol/L, LFTs mildly deranged with ALT 68 U/L.

The medical team has been asked to plan refeeding. She has been eating minimal food for two weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 42, blood pressure 88/54 lying and 74/48 standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 35.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), glucose 3.2 mmol/L, ALT 68 U/L
data_table.ECG: sinus bradycardia 42, QTc 460 ms, prominent U waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate refeeding plan?

options.text: Withhold all nutrition for 48 hours to allow gradual electrolyte normalisation then start at 15 kcal/kg/day with oral supplements once stable
options.rationale: Prolonged starvation while inpatient worsens outcomes; the correct approach is early low-energy refeeding with concurrent electrolyte and thiamine cover, not further fasting. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Commence a standard maintenance diet at 30 kcal/kg/day today with oral supplementation and correct electrolytes only if levels fall further
options.rationale: Full maintenance energy in a very high refeeding risk patient causes acute refeeding syndrome (cardiac failure, arrhythmia, Wernicke encephalopathy); start slow and correct pre-emptively. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and deliver 100 percent of estimated caloric needs immediately by continuous feed to accelerate weight restoration
options.rationale: Continuous full-target NG feeding in severe undernutrition precipitates refeeding syndrome; NG feeding is used when oral intake is inadequate but starts at low energy with slow escalation. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Give a rapid IV glucose bolus of 200 mL 10 percent dextrose to correct hypoglycaemia, then start standard diet at full maintenance today
options.rationale: IV glucose without thiamine cover risks Wernicke encephalopathy; hypoglycaemia in anorexia is corrected with oral or small enteral carbohydrate after thiamine, not rapid IV boluses in a stable patient. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Start oral thiamine 200 mg daily, correct electrolyte deficits first, then commence energy at 20 kcal/kg/day and increase over 5 to 7 days
options.rationale: Severe anorexia (BMI 12.8) with hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphataemia is at very high refeeding risk; start thiamine BEFORE any carbohydrate, replace electrolytes, then commence low energy (10 to 20 kcal/kg/day) with slow uptitration and daily electrolyte monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is triggered by carbohydrate reintroduction after starvation, driving insulin release and rapid intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, causing arrhythmia, cardiac failure, Wernicke encephalopathy, and death. Very high risk criteria (NICE): BMI under 14, minimal intake over 15 days, weight loss over 20 percent, or existing hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia or hypophosphataemia. Start thiamine before glucose, replace electrolytes pre-emptively, start energy low (10 to 20 kcal/kg/day) with slow escalation and daily monitoring.
key_points: Thiamine 200 to 300 mg PO daily BEFORE any carbohydrate
Correct K, Mg, PO4 pre-emptively and daily
Start energy at 10 to 20 kcal/kg/day, uptitrate over 5 to 7 days
Cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia in first week
explanation.pearls: MARSIPAN/AN-CHECK Australian criteria for medical admission: BMI <13, pulse <40, systolic BP <80, postural drop >20 mmHg, temperature <35.5 C, potassium <3.0. Any one is grounds for medical stabilisation.

subtopic_detail: Acute-on-chronic lithium toxicity with renal impairment
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 62-year-old woman with a 25-year history of bipolar I on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for maintenance. She started ramipril 10 mg for hypertension 3 weeks ago and had a gastroenteritis 4 days ago. Her family brought her in because she has been increasingly confused, tremulous, and unsteady over 48 hours. On examination she is drowsy (GCS 12), coarse tremor of both hands, hyperreflexia, myoclonic jerks, ataxia. She is not febrile.

Bloods: lithium level 3.4 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6 to 1.0), sodium 148 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L, creatinine 216 umol/L (baseline 78 six months ago), eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. TFTs normal. Anion gap normal. ECG shows sinus rhythm at 92 with T-wave flattening and one PVC per 10 beats.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: lithium 3.4 mmol/L (0.6-1.0 therapeutic), sodium 148 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 216 umol/L (baseline 78), eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2
data_table.Neuro: GCS 12, coarse tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, ataxia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold lithium, commence IV 0.9 percent saline at maintenance plus 5 percent deficit, and refer to renal for urgent haemodialysis
options.rationale: Lithium above 2.5 mmol/L with severe neurological features (altered consciousness, myoclonus, ataxia) or above 4.0 mmol/L regardless of symptoms, especially with renal impairment reducing excretion, is an indication for haemodialysis. Withhold lithium and provide IV saline while dialysis is arranged. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Give IV activated charcoal 50 g nasogastrically to reduce further lithium absorption before further specific management
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium (it is an ionic salt with poor charcoal affinity) and is contraindicated in reduced GCS without a secure airway; dialysis is the correct removal method. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence forced alkaline diuresis with intravenous sodium bicarbonate to accelerate renal lithium clearance
options.rationale: Forced alkaline diuresis is not the treatment for lithium toxicity; lithium is not weak-acid protein-bound. IV saline is used to restore volume and improve excretion, and haemodialysis is required in severe cases. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue lithium at a reduced dose of 250 mg nocte and add oral quetiapine 50 mg for symptomatic control while awaiting stabilisation
options.rationale: Continuing lithium in severe toxicity with renal impairment is dangerous; complete withdrawal until level and renal function normalise is required. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Give intravenous physostigmine 2 mg to reverse the anticholinergic effects contributing to her acute confusional state
options.rationale: Lithium toxicity is not anticholinergic; physostigmine has no role and may cause bradyarrhythmia and seizure. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity is precipitated by dehydration, renal impairment, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides, NSAIDs, or dose error. Severity is not solely by level: chronic toxicity may have neurological features at lower levels than acute overdose. Indications for haemodialysis (EXTRIP criteria): level over 4.0 mmol/L regardless of symptoms, level over 2.5 mmol/L with severe neurological features or renal impairment, or level over 2.5 with expected clearance time above 36 hours. Withhold lithium, IV saline for volume, seizure precautions, and refer to renal.
key_points: Withhold lithium; IV 0.9% saline to restore volume
Haemodialysis indicated: level >4.0, or >2.5 with severe symptoms or renal impairment
Charcoal does NOT bind lithium; not indicated
Screen for ACEi/ARB/thiazide/NSAID interaction
