explanation.pearls: EXTRIP working group thresholds are widely adopted. Rebound rise after dialysis is common due to redistribution; monitor 6- to 12-hourly levels and repeat dialysis if rebound >1.0 with symptoms.

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on-call reviewing a 42-year-old man admitted 48 hours ago after presenting acutely psychotic and agitated. He was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg BD and lorazepam 2 mg TDS. He has a background of major depressive disorder for which he takes citalopram 40 mg, and his GP added tramadol 100 mg TDS two weeks ago for back pain. Overnight he became increasingly restless, developed generalised tremor, and vomited twice.

On examination: temperature 38.6, pulse 128, blood pressure 168/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96 percent on room air. He is alert and oriented but confused. Pupils are 6 mm, reactive. Marked lower-limb hyperreflexia with inducible ankle clonus (6 beats) and spontaneous myoclonic jerks. Increased tone in the legs more than the arms. Bowel sounds hyperactive. Diaphoretic. CK 220 U/L (below 170).

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 168/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: CK 220 U/L (<170), WCC 10.4 x10^9/L, creatinine 84 umol/L, lithium not applicable
data_table.Neuro: 6 mm reactive pupils, lower limb hyperreflexia > upper, inducible ankle clonus 6 beats, myoclonic jerks, diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; stop olanzapine, commence dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV and bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally
options.rationale: NMS is characterised by lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, sluggish pupils, bradykinesia, marked CK rise, and normal or reduced bowel sounds; the picture here (lower limb hyperreflexia, clonus, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds, mild CK rise) is classic serotonin syndrome. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Serotonin syndrome; cease citalopram and tramadol, provide supportive care with IV fluids and benzodiazepines, add cyproheptadine 12 mg orally if severe
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria: use of serotonergic agent plus spontaneous or inducible clonus with agitation, diaphoresis or hyperthermia, or ocular clonus) here from citalopram plus tramadol combination; treat by ceasing serotonergic agents, aggressive supportive care with benzodiazepines and fluids, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally in moderate to severe cases. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Anticholinergic toxidrome; give physostigmine 2 mg IV and monitor cardiac rhythm continuously until symptoms resolve
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxidrome causes dry skin, mydriasis, absent bowel sounds, and urinary retention; diaphoresis and hyperactive bowel sounds argue against and physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Sympathomimetic toxidrome from illicit stimulant use; administer IV benzodiazepines only and observe for clinical improvement
options.rationale: Sympathomimetic (cocaine, methamphetamine) toxidrome shares hyperthermia and hypertension but does not cause clonus and lower-limb-predominant hyperreflexia; the temporal association with citalopram and tramadol makes serotonin syndrome the diagnosis. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Malignant hyperthermia; give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV every 5 minutes and active surface cooling with ice packs and fanning
options.rationale: Malignant hyperthermia is an anaesthetic emergency triggered by volatile agents or succinylcholine, with masseter spasm and severe hyperthermia; it does not fit this clinical picture with no anaesthesia exposure. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome and NMS can look similar but differ in key ways. Serotonin syndrome (SS): rapid onset after adding or increasing a serotonergic agent, lower limb hyperreflexia with clonus (spontaneous or inducible), mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds, diaphoresis, and mild-moderate CK rise. NMS: subacute (24 to 72 h), lead-pipe rigidity throughout, hyporeflexia, sluggish pupils, absent bowel sounds, marked CK rise (often over 1000). Treatment: cease offending drug; SS uses benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine; NMS uses dantrolene and bromocriptine.
key_points: SS: clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, hyperactive gut, sweaty, mild CK rise
NMS: rigid, hyporeflexic, sluggish pupils, absent gut, high CK
SS treatment: cease drug, IV fluids, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine 12 mg PO for moderate/severe
NMS treatment: cease drug, IV fluids, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg, bromocriptine 2.5 mg PO
explanation.pearls: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria: use of serotonergic agent plus 1 of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; tremor and hyperreflexia; hypertonia + temp >38 C + ocular or inducible clonus.

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder in crisis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on-call in ED reviewing a 27-year-old woman brought by ambulance after making superficial parallel cuts to her left forearm. She has known borderline personality disorder, is engaged with a public mental health service where she attends weekly DBT skills group and monthly psychiatrist review. She has 14 prior admissions for self-harm and one prior serious attempt with paracetamol overdose 3 years ago. Tonight she cut after an argument with her partner. She has not consumed alcohol or drugs.

On assessment she is calm, engaged, and future-oriented. She apologises for coming in and says she used all her DBT skills first, only cut after they failed. She wants to go home. She has no active plan, has removed the razor blades from her flat, has agreed to phone her case manager tomorrow morning, and will attend group later this week. Her partner is present, supportive, and can stay with her overnight. Wounds do not require sutures.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Assessment: calm, engaged, apologetic, future-oriented, denies active plan, DBT-engaged, safety plan in place, partner supportive
data_table.Wound: 3 superficial parallel forearm cuts, no bleeding, dressed, no suture needed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act to a psychiatric ward for observation given the pattern of repeated self-harm
options.rationale: Involuntary admission for chronic self-harm in stable BPD is generally harmful (institutional dependency, reinforcement of admission-as-solution) and does not meet MHA criteria when there is engagement, no active intent, and adequate community support. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Refer for a 6 to 8 week course of ECT to reduce her recurrent affective dysregulation and self-harm behaviours
options.rationale: ECT has no role in BPD unless there is a co-occurring severe treatment-resistant major depressive episode; it is not indicated for the personality disorder itself. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Admit voluntarily to a psychiatric ward for a 3 to 5 day break and commence olanzapine 5 mg for affective instability during admission
options.rationale: Brief admissions for BPD are unhelpful and pharmacotherapy adds side effects without evidence of benefit; medication targets specific comorbidities, not the personality diagnosis itself. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Discharge with a joint written safety plan, contact her case manager tomorrow, and arrange next scheduled DBT session as planned this week
options.rationale: Chronic BPD self-harm without acute imminent risk is best managed in the community with existing supports; admission is not therapeutic for chronic suicidality and disrupts the DBT frame. Discharge with a documented safety plan, early follow-up, and use of established supports is the evidence-based approach. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Prescribe short-course diazepam 5 mg TDS for 2 weeks and increase her SSRI dose empirically to reduce chronic self-harm behaviour
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are contraindicated in BPD (worsen disinhibition and impulsive self-harm); SSRI titration for BPD chronic self-harm is not evidence-based unless treating a defined depressive episode. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

explanation.summary: Chronic self-harm in stable BPD is best managed in the community with an existing therapeutic frame (DBT, MBT, or schema therapy). Admission does not reduce long-term suicide risk and often reinforces admission-as-coping. Discharge is appropriate when the patient is future-oriented, has engaged with skills first, has means restriction, has follow-up scheduled, and has social support. Admission is reserved for co-occurring acute severe MDD, acute psychosis, acute intoxication, or a clear change in trajectory suggesting shift to imminent lethality.
key_points: Chronic self-harm in stable BPD: community management with safety plan
Admission indications: acute severe MDD, psychosis, intoxication, clear escalation
Avoid benzodiazepines (disinhibition), pharmacotherapy targets comorbidity
Structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, SFT, TFT) is first-line
explanation.pearls: Australian NHMRC BPD guideline (2013, still current) emphasises psychological therapies as primary treatment; medication only for specific comorbid mood or psychotic symptoms. Admissions if used should be brief and goal-focused.

subtopic_detail: Bipolar I depressive episode pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder (diagnosed at 22, 3 prior manic episodes, 4 prior depressive episodes) currently in a 5-week depressive episode. She has low mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia (sleeping 12 to 14 hours), psychomotor slowing, guilt, poor concentration, and passive suicidal thoughts without plan. She stopped lithium 4 months ago because she disliked hand tremor and lost weight. She has never taken an antidepressant.

Her weight is 68 kg, BMI 24. Thyroid function normal, U&Es normal (eGFR over 90), creatinine 62 umol/L. Her most recent manic episode was 3 years ago on lithium monotherapy at level 0.6 mmol/L; she was hospitalised for two weeks. She and her husband are planning a pregnancy in the next 12 to 18 months.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: TSH 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine 62 umol/L, eGFR >90, calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), pregnancy test negative
data_table.History: bipolar I, 3 manic and 4 depressive episodes, off lithium 4 months, planning pregnancy 12-18 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy for this depressive episode?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg nocte plus fluoxetine 20 mg daily (OFC combination) as first-line for the current bipolar depressive episode
options.rationale: OFC is effective for bipolar depression but not first-line preferred in pregnancy planning due to metabolic and teratogenic concerns; lithium or lamotrigine are preferred initial choices with clear prior response. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg alone with no mood stabiliser cover because the priority is treating the acute depressive episode symptomatically
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar I depression risks switch to mania and rapid cycling; mood stabiliser cover is required if any antidepressant is used, and antidepressant use in bipolar I is limited. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 500 mg BD as monotherapy for both mood stabilisation and treatment of the depressive episode she now has
options.rationale: Valproate is highly teratogenic (neural tube defects, autism spectrum, IQ reduction) and is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy under the pregnancy prevention program; not appropriate here. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Commence carbamazepine 200 mg BD as first-line mood stabiliser and add fluoxetine 20 mg for the current depressive symptomatology
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is second-line for bipolar and is a teratogen (neural tube defects, oral clefts) requiring reliable contraception; fluoxetine monotherapy risks manic switch. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Restart lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte alone, target level 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L, and involve reproductive psychiatry for pregnancy planning
options.rationale: Lithium is a first-line treatment for bipolar depression with strong evidence for both depression and prophylaxis and prior demonstrated response; her prior tremor and weight loss are manageable. Preconception counselling weighs cardiac malformation risk (Ebstein anomaly ~1 in 1000 to 2000) versus recurrence risk in pregnancy. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

explanation.summary: First-line options for bipolar I depression include lithium, quetiapine, and lamotrigine (slower onset), each with evidence and specific considerations. Lithium suits a patient with prior response, adequate renal function, and long-term prophylactic need, with the pregnancy-planning discussion including Ebstein anomaly risk (~1 in 1000 to 2000 with first trimester exposure) versus untreated bipolar recurrence risk (approximately 50 percent in pregnancy and postpartum). Antidepressant monotherapy is avoided in bipolar I because of the switch risk.
key_points: First-line for bipolar depression: lithium, quetiapine, lamotrigine
Avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar I (switch to mania)
Valproate contraindicated in women of reproductive age unless in PPP
Preconception counselling: risk of untreated illness vs teratogenicity
explanation.pearls: CANMAT 2018 first-line for bipolar I depression: quetiapine, lurasidone, lithium, lamotrigine, and lithium/lamotrigine combined; olanzapine-fluoxetine second-line. Ebstein anomaly risk with first trimester lithium ~1 in 1000 to 2000, up from baseline 1 in 20000.

subtopic_detail: Postnatal depression identified at 6-week check
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 32-year-old primiparous woman at her routine 6-week postnatal check. Her baby is thriving and exclusively breastfed. She scored 15 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) today (positive 13 or above), scoring 1 on item 10 (thought of harming self). She reports 4 weeks of persistent low mood, tearfulness most days, sleep disruption beyond baby's feeds, feeling overwhelmed, and reduced enjoyment of her baby. She denies thoughts of harming the baby. There is no personal history of psychiatric illness. Her mother had postnatal depression.

She has no active suicidal plan or intent, no psychotic features, no acute safety concerns. Her partner is supportive and present. Social support is intact. Physical examination and thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), FBC and iron studies unremarkable
data_table.Assessment: EPDS 15, item 10 score 1 (occasional thoughts, no active plan), no psychosis, partner supportive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Advise her to stop breastfeeding immediately so that safe pharmacotherapy can be commenced without concern for infant exposure
options.rationale: Breastfeeding cessation is not required to treat PND; SSRIs including sertraline are safe with breastfeeding with minimal infant exposure. Discouraging breastfeeding worsens outcomes for both mother and baby. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal MH)

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg titrated to 50 mg daily monotherapy alone for depression without any psychological therapy referral in first-line management
options.rationale: SSRI monotherapy without psychological therapy is not first-line for moderate PND in a woman who has not previously tried psychological therapy; combined therapy is more effective than either alone if medication is used. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal MH)

options.text: Refer for structured psychological therapy (interpersonal therapy or CBT) with GP review in 2 weeks and safety plan for any escalation
options.rationale: Moderate postnatal depression (EPDS 15, no psychosis, no active suicidal intent) responds well to structured psychological therapy (interpersonal therapy or CBT) as first-line with GP follow-up. Medication is added if psychological therapy alone is insufficient or severity increases. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal MH)

options.text: Admit to a mother-baby unit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act for immediate psychiatric assessment and stabilisation
options.rationale: Involuntary admission for moderate PND without psychosis, active suicidal intent, or safety concern is disproportionate and not appropriate; her presentation is community-manageable with structured supports. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal MH)

options.text: Reassure her that this is baby blues and will resolve spontaneously in the next 2 weeks; follow up if not improving
options.rationale: Baby blues resolve within 10 to 14 days of delivery; symptoms lasting 4 weeks with EPDS 15 meet threshold for depression and require active management rather than reassurance. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal MH)

explanation.summary: The 6-week postnatal check is a national screening opportunity using EPDS. Score 13 or above suggests significant depressive symptoms warranting further assessment; item 10 (self-harm thoughts) requires safety assessment regardless of total score. Moderate PND is managed first-line with structured psychological therapy (interpersonal therapy or CBT); sertraline is the preferred SSRI if medication is added, being compatible with breastfeeding. Severe PND, psychotic features, or active suicidal or infanticidal thoughts warrant urgent perinatal psychiatry referral and consideration of mother-baby unit admission.
key_points: EPDS >=13 or item 10 positive: further assessment
First-line moderate PND: psychological therapy (IPT or CBT)
SSRI first choice if medication: sertraline (compatible with breastfeeding)
Escalate to perinatal psychiatry for severe, psychotic, or high-risk presentations
explanation.pearls: Sertraline lowest breastmilk transfer of SSRIs; paroxetine also low transfer. Fluoxetine has long half-life and higher infant plasma levels: avoid if starting anew in a lactating woman.

subtopic_detail: 17 year old cannabis user with 3 months of delusions and functional decline
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 17-year-old boy referred by his GP with 3 months of persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, and withdrawal from school. He has been using cannabis 4 times a week since age 15. His mother describes him as flat, suspicious, and staying awake at night. There is no substance intoxication currently and no acute suicidality or violence. He has no medical comorbidity. Physical examination and bloods are normal. He is engaged with his mother and willing to try treatment.

He is being seen in the Early Intervention Service outpatient clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, weight 68 kg
data_table.Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT normal, urine drug screen positive cannabis only, HbA1c 33 mmol/mol, prolactin 320 mIU/L (males under 350)
data_table.Imaging: MRI brain unremarkable, ECG QTc 400 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: SSRI sertraline 50 mg orally daily as first line because cannabis-induced anxiety underlies the presentation
options.rationale: SSRIs do not treat psychotic symptoms and may worsen them in cannabis induced psychosis; antipsychotic therapy plus cessation support is standard first line. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guideline)

options.text: Olanzapine 20 mg orally at night at full target dose from day one to control positive symptoms rapidly
options.rationale: Olanzapine at high starting dose has significant metabolic risk (weight, glucose, lipids) in adolescents; start low and titrate slowly, and it is not first choice for FEP. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guideline)

options.text: Haloperidol 10 mg orally daily and lithium 800 mg orally at night for mood stabilisation as first therapy
options.rationale: First generation antipsychotics have higher extrapyramidal side effects than second generation, and adding lithium without a clear mood diagnosis is inappropriate. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guideline)

options.text: Clozapine 12.5 mg orally at night and titrate over 2 weeks alongside weekly full blood count monitoring
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after failure of two adequate trials of other antipsychotics; it is not first line in FEP. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guideline)

options.text: Risperidone 1 mg orally at night with slow titration to 2 to 4 mg daily, plus psychosocial support in EIS
options.rationale: First episode psychosis in adolescents is treated with low dose second-generation antipsychotic (risperidone 1 to 4 mg or aripiprazole 5 to 15 mg) with slow titration to minimise side effects, alongside evidence-based psychosocial intervention through EIS. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guideline)

explanation.summary: First episode psychosis in adolescents is treated with a low dose second-generation antipsychotic (typically risperidone or aripiprazole) titrated slowly, alongside psychosocial intervention through the Early Intervention Service. Olanzapine is avoided as first line due to metabolic side effects. Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistance. Baseline metabolic parameters and ECG are checked and monitored. Cannabis cessation support is essential.
key_points: First line: low dose second-generation antipsychotic (risperidone, aripiprazole)
Start low, titrate slowly, watch metabolic and EPS side effects
Clozapine after 2 adequate antipsychotic trials fail
EIS provides case management, family work, and CBTp
explanation.pearls: RANZCP recommends baseline weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, and ECG before starting antipsychotic; risperidone dose in adolescents starts 0.5 to 1 mg, target 2 to 4 mg, higher doses give more EPS without extra efficacy.

subtopic_detail: CIWA 22 with tremor and tachycardia at day 2
stem:
You are the psychiatry consultation liaison registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man 36 hours after admission to a medical ward for pancreatitis. He drinks 200 g alcohol daily. He is tremulous, sweating, agitated, and disoriented to time. Heart rate is 128 and blood pressure 168/98. He has had a single 5 mg IV diazepam so far. CIWA-Ar score is now 22. Blood alcohol is zero. He has no seizure yet. Magnesium is 0.62, potassium 3.4. He is nil by mouth for pancreatitis.

The medical team asks about withdrawal management.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 168/98, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.5 degrees Celsius, weight 82 kg
data_table.Bloods: sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), glucose 6.2 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), lipase 780 U/L (10-60), CK 240 U/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV diazepam 10 mg boluses every 15 minutes until CIWA under 10, plus IV thiamine 300 mg daily and magnesium replacement
options.rationale: Severe alcohol withdrawal is treated with symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (front loading with IV diazepam boluses), IV high dose thiamine before any glucose, and correction of magnesium and potassium to reduce seizure and DT risk. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: Oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg 6 hourly fixed schedule for 5 days and oral thiamine 100 mg once daily
options.rationale: Oral fixed schedule is inappropriate when nil by mouth for pancreatitis, and low oral thiamine dose is insufficient in high risk withdrawal; symptom-triggered IV benzodiazepine and high dose parenteral thiamine are indicated. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg IM to sedate the agitation without further benzodiazepine
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and do not treat withdrawal; benzodiazepines are the primary agent for alcohol withdrawal management. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV dextrose 50 percent 50 mL bolus first for hypoglycaemia risk then thiamine 100 mg IV over 2 hours after
options.rationale: Giving glucose before thiamine in a chronic alcohol user risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine must be given first or concurrently. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV clonidine 150 mcg boluses only to lower blood pressure and pulse, without benzodiazepine or thiamine therapy
options.rationale: Clonidine treats autonomic symptoms but not seizure or delirium risk; it is adjunctive at most, benzodiazepines and thiamine are essential first line. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe alcohol withdrawal is managed with symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (front-loaded diazepam boluses to CIWA-Ar under 10), IV thiamine before or with any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and correction of magnesium and potassium. Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and are not first line. Clonidine treats autonomic symptoms but not seizures or delirium. Anti-emetics may be used adjunctively.
key_points: Benzodiazepines are first line for alcohol withdrawal (diazepam or lorazepam)
Thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 3 to 5 days before any glucose
Correct magnesium and potassium to reduce seizure risk
Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are not first line
explanation.pearls: CIWA-Ar over 15 signals severe withdrawal; diazepam has long active metabolites providing smooth taper, lorazepam preferred in significant hepatic impairment; risk factors for DTs include prior DT or seizure, tachycardia over 120, systolic BP over 160, and high blood alcohol on presentation still drinking.

subtopic_detail: Generalised tonic clonic seizure at day 3 of withdrawal on the ward
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to a 60-year-old man on day 3 of an admission for alcohol withdrawal. He has just had a witnessed 90 second generalised tonic clonic seizure. He is now post-ictal and confused with GCS 12. He was on oral diazepam 10 mg 6 hourly as needed. He is diaphoretic, tremulous, and tachycardic. He has had no vomiting and airway is patent. Point-of-care glucose is 4.6 and sodium is 132. Magnesium is 0.55. He has no head injury. He is being nursed in a general medical bay.

The consultant is on their way. You must act now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 172/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius, GCS 12 post-ictal
data_table.Bloods: sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.55 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), ethanol 0 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: CT brain arranged non-urgently after stabilisation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV phenytoin 20 mg per kg loading dose infused over 30 minutes and continue oral diazepam as previously prescribed
options.rationale: Phenytoin is ineffective for alcohol withdrawal seizures because the mechanism is GABA hypofunction, not neuronal hyperexcitability; benzodiazepine is first line. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV lorazepam 4 mg bolus now with airway support, IV thiamine 300 mg, IV magnesium 10 mmol over 1 hour, transfer to HDU
options.rationale: Alcohol withdrawal seizure is treated with IV benzodiazepine, high dose parenteral thiamine, magnesium and potassium replacement, and escalation of care due to DT risk; lorazepam has active metabolites less affected by hepatic dysfunction. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV levetiracetam 60 mg per kg loading dose alone and no additional benzodiazepine for the withdrawal seizure now
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is used in status epilepticus of other causes; alcohol withdrawal seizure needs benzodiazepine, not levetiracetam as sole therapy. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV thiopental 3 mg per kg for immediate seizure abortion and paralysis with rocuronium for tracheal intubation
options.rationale: Thiopental induction and paralysis is not indicated for a single self-terminated withdrawal seizure with intact airway; benzodiazepine and supportive care are the correct step. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg and lorazepam 1 mg IM to manage agitation, and defer thiamine until confirmed nutritional status
options.rationale: Haloperidol lowers seizure threshold; withholding thiamine risks Wernicke encephalopathy. Prompt IV thiamine is essential in this scenario. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal seizures are treated with IV benzodiazepines (lorazepam or diazepam), high dose parenteral thiamine, and correction of magnesium and potassium. Phenytoin and levetiracetam do not treat the underlying GABA hypofunction and are ineffective. Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are avoided. After a withdrawal seizure the risk of DTs and further seizures rises so escalation to HDU is prudent.
key_points: First line for withdrawal seizure: IV benzodiazepine
IV thiamine 300 mg before or with any glucose
Correct magnesium and potassium promptly
Phenytoin and levetiracetam are not effective for withdrawal seizures
explanation.pearls: Prior withdrawal seizure is the strongest single risk factor for DTs (risk about 3 fold); RACGP suggests loading IV diazepam 20 mg every 20 minutes up to 100 mg or lorazepam 4 mg every 15 minutes titrated to symptoms; consider phenobarbital for benzodiazepine resistant DTs in ICU.

subtopic_detail: Persistent orofacial dyskinesia after 5 years of antipsychotic therapy
stem:
You are the community psychiatrist reviewing a 58-year-old woman with schizophrenia stable on risperidone 4 mg daily for 5 years. She has developed persistent tongue protrusion, lip smacking, and choreoathetoid movements of her fingers over the past 6 months. The Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale score is 12. She has not had recent dose changes. She is not depressed and functioning well socially. Reducing or switching antipsychotic in the past has caused relapse. She is on no other movement affecting medication.

She finds the movements distressing.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, weight 76 kg
data_table.Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, calcium and copper normal, HbA1c 41 mmol/mol, prolactin 620 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Add propranolol 40 mg orally three times daily and continue current antipsychotic without switching agent
options.rationale: Propranolol treats akathisia, not tardive dyskinesia; it has no established role in TD reduction. (Source: APA Schizophrenia Guideline 2020)

options.text: Add oral benzatropine 2 mg orally twice daily as anticholinergic therapy for the involuntary movements now
options.rationale: Anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia; they are used for acute dystonia or parkinsonism only and are contraindicated in TD. (Source: APA Schizophrenia Guideline 2020)

options.text: Add valbenazine 40 mg orally once daily, uptitrate to 80 mg after 1 week if tolerated and monitor for sedation
options.rationale: VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are first line evidence-based treatment for moderate to severe tardive dyskinesia; they reduce AIMS scores with tolerable side effects. (Source: APA Schizophrenia Guideline 2020)

options.text: Increase risperidone dose to 6 mg orally daily to suppress the movements and manage residual psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: Increasing the offending agent temporarily masks TD but worsens the underlying process; long term worsening is expected and it is not standard care. (Source: APA Schizophrenia Guideline 2020)

options.text: Switch to clozapine 12.5 mg orally at night with weekly full blood count first line as best option for TD control
options.rationale: Clozapine may be considered when TD coexists with treatment resistant psychosis, but is not first line for TD when the patient is stable on current antipsychotic; VMAT2 inhibitor is first line. (Source: APA Schizophrenia Guideline 2020)

explanation.summary: Tardive dyskinesia after long term antipsychotic use is treated first line with a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine) when clinically significant. Anticholinergics worsen TD and propranolol treats akathisia, not TD. Increasing the offending antipsychotic worsens TD long term. Clozapine may help when TD coexists with treatment resistant psychosis. Regular AIMS monitoring guides therapy.
key_points: VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are first line for TD
Anticholinergics worsen TD
Increasing the offending antipsychotic worsens TD long term
AIMS monitoring at baseline and 3 to 6 monthly on antipsychotic
explanation.pearls: Valbenazine dose 40 mg starting, uptitrate to 80 mg after 1 week, watch for somnolence, QTc prolongation and parkinsonism; deutetrabenazine 6 mg twice daily starting, target 18 to 24 mg twice daily; monitor AIMS every 3 months on treatment.

subtopic_detail: Severe depression with psychosis and food refusal, prior medication failure
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman admitted involuntarily for severe depression with mood congruent psychotic delusions of decay and 4 weeks of food and fluid refusal. She has lost 12 kg. She has failed adequate trials of sertraline and mirtazapine over 6 months. She is now dehydrated, bradycardic, and mute. Blood tests show mild AKI. She has capacity assessed as impaired for treatment decisions. Her adult daughter is her formally appointed medical treatment decision maker and consents to ECT. There are no contraindications.

An anaesthetist has assessed her and approves ECT under general anaesthetic.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 56, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius, weight 52 kg (was 64 kg)
data_table.Bloods: sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 128 umol/L (45-90), ECG sinus bradycardia QTc 420 ms
data_table.Imaging: CT brain no acute pathology or mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: IV ketamine 0.5 mg per kg over 40 minutes weekly in outpatient clinic as first line therapy after medication failure
options.rationale: Ketamine for depression is second line and not established for severe depression with psychosis; safety in acute inpatient severe illness is limited compared with ECT. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guideline)

options.text: Trial venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily uptitrating over 4 weeks before considering electroconvulsive therapy referral
options.rationale: In severe depression with psychosis, food refusal, and medication failure, further oral antidepressant trial delays life-saving treatment; ECT has response within 2 to 3 weeks and is first line here. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guideline)

options.text: Add lithium 400 mg orally at night augmentation of current SSRI as first step before any ECT is considered
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is one option in TRD, but not appropriate as first step when the patient is deteriorating rapidly with food refusal; ECT is faster acting and indicated. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guideline)

options.text: Start twice weekly bitemporal ECT with 6 to 12 sessions expected, rehydrate first, prescribe pre-ECT metoclopramide and monitor cognition
options.rationale: Severe depression with psychosis, food refusal, and medication failure is a strong indication for ECT; twice weekly bitemporal or high dose right unilateral is standard; rehydration and pre-ECT preparation reduce anaesthetic risk. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guideline)

options.text: IV clomipramine 25 mg daily infusion titrated up over 10 days as intravenous antidepressant instead of ECT
options.rationale: IV clomipramine is not standard in Australia and lacks evidence over oral therapy or ECT; ECT is faster and safer in this clinical picture. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe depression with psychotic features, catatonia, food refusal, or high suicide risk after failed medication trials is a first line indication for ECT, which acts within 2 to 3 weeks. Bitemporal placement gives fastest and most potent effect but with more cognitive side effects; high dose right unilateral is an alternative with less memory impact. Rehydration and pre-ECT assessment reduce anaesthetic risk. Ongoing maintenance may be pharmacological or continuation ECT.
key_points: First line ECT indications: severe depression with psychosis, catatonia, food refusal, high suicide risk
Response usually within 6 to 12 sessions, given twice weekly
Bitemporal fastest response, right unilateral less cognitive impact
Consent required from patient or medical treatment decision maker if impaired
explanation.pearls: RANZCP audit shows response rates 60 to 80 percent in TRD; number needed to treat around 2 for remission in severe psychotic depression; short term memory effects usually resolve in 6 months, long term autobiographical gaps rare with unilateral placement.

subtopic_detail: Chronic post traumatic stress with dissociation after childhood abuse
stem:
You are the psychiatry consultant reviewing a 34-year-old woman with 10 years of intrusive memories, dissociative episodes, chronic nightmares, hyperarousal, and unstable relationships since childhood sexual abuse. She has tried sertraline for 6 months at 200 mg with partial response. She is stable psychosocially with supportive partner and no active substance use. She has no current suicidal intent but self-harmed 6 months ago. She wants to reduce dissociation and nightmares. She has read about EMDR and asks whether it might help her.

She is engaged and prefers a structured psychological approach.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, weight 68 kg
data_table.Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT normal, HbA1c 34 mmol/mol, no substance use on urine screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her care?

options.text: Refer for supportive counselling only and continue current sertraline without additional pharmacological or psychological therapy
options.rationale: Non-trauma-focused counselling has weaker evidence than TF-CBT or EMDR in PTSD; the recommended approach is trauma-focused psychological therapy. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Switch sertraline to venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily and add quetiapine 100 mg at night for dissociation control
options.rationale: Second SSRI or SNRI switch is reasonable in nonresponse but should be paired with trauma-focused therapy; quetiapine is not first line for dissociation and adds metabolic risk without established PTSD benefit. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Start clonazepam 0.5 mg at night for hyperarousal and defer psychological therapy until symptoms are controlled first
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes and impair trauma processing; they are contraindicated as monotherapy in PTSD. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Add mirtazapine 30 mg at night for sleep and continue sertraline without any psychological intervention referral
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy alone leaves PTSD undertreated; trauma-focused psychological therapy is the strongest evidence-based treatment and should be offered. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for trauma-focused psychological therapy (either EMDR or trauma-focused CBT), and add prazosin 1 mg at night for nightmares
options.rationale: Trauma-focused psychological therapies (TF-CBT or EMDR) are first line for PTSD in Australian and international guidelines, alongside SSRI; prazosin is second line adjunct for trauma nightmares in adults. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: PTSD treatment in adults is trauma-focused psychological therapy (TF-CBT or EMDR) as first line, with SSRI (sertraline or paroxetine) or venlafaxine as pharmacological options. Prazosin is a second line adjunct for trauma related nightmares. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated. Complex PTSD after childhood trauma may need longer and phased therapy. Supportive counselling alone has weaker evidence than trauma-focused approaches.
key_points: First line: trauma-focused psychological therapy (TF-CBT or EMDR)
Pharmacological first line: SSRI (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine
Prazosin second line adjunct for trauma related nightmares
Avoid benzodiazepines: worsen PTSD outcomes
explanation.pearls: Phoenix Australia recommends 8 to 12 sessions of TF-CBT or EMDR for uncomplicated PTSD, phased approach with stabilisation before trauma processing in complex PTSD; prazosin start 1 mg at night, titrate to 2 to 6 mg for nightmares, watch first-dose hypotension.

subtopic_detail: Treatment intensity selection when psychosis is mood-congruent
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health team reviewing a 52-year-old man referred by his general practitioner after 6 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, early morning waking, 4 kg weight loss, and psychomotor retardation. In the last week he has developed the belief that his liver is rotting and that he does not deserve to eat. He denies command hallucinations and current suicidal plan but describes passive death wishes. He is a lawyer with previously good function. He has no prior mental health history and is not on any medications.

His wife has taken time off work to stay with him and is present with him today.

data_table.MSE: flat affect, thought content includes nihilistic delusion (rotting liver), passive death wish, no perceptual disturbance elicited
data_table.Bloods: urea, electrolytes, LFTs, TSH, B12, folate within normal limits
data_table.Weight: 4 kg loss over 6 weeks, currently 68 kg
data_table.Suicide risk: no plan, no means, passive death wish, wife providing support

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily as monotherapy with follow up in 2 weeks in the community mental health team clinic setting
options.rationale: SSRI monotherapy is inadequate for depression with psychotic features; RANZCOG-endorsed RANZCP mood disorder guidance recommends antidepressant plus antipsychotic combination or ECT. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone with medication review deferred until 6 sessions have been completed
options.rationale: CBT alone is inappropriate first-line for severe depression with psychotic features; combined pharmacotherapy or ECT is standard, with psychological therapy added later. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Combined sertraline 50 mg with olanzapine 5 mg nocte, admission for observation and safety planning with the wife
options.rationale: Depression with psychotic features requires combined antidepressant plus antipsychotic (or ECT); admission with safety planning is prudent given nihilistic delusions and passive death wishes even without an active plan. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg monotherapy nocte for the psychotic symptoms with weekly community follow up appointments
options.rationale: Antipsychotic monotherapy without an antidepressant fails to treat the depressive syndrome; combined therapy (or ECT) is standard for psychotic depression. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 5 mg three times daily for sleep and anxiety while awaiting outpatient psychiatry review appointment
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are adjuncts for insomnia or agitation but do not treat depression or psychosis; delay in initiating definitive treatment risks progression. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Depression with psychotic features is a severe subtype in which delusions (often mood-congruent: nihilistic, guilt, poverty, somatic) and sometimes hallucinations occur. First-line is combined antidepressant plus atypical antipsychotic (e.g. SSRI plus olanzapine or quetiapine), or electroconvulsive therapy for severe cases with high suicide risk, refusal of food, or severe agitation. Admission is warranted when safety, self-care, or supervision cannot be assured at home. Response is typically assessed at 4-6 weeks; combination therapy is continued for at least 6 months after remission.
key_points: Combined antidepressant plus antipsychotic (or ECT) is first-line
ECT preferred when catatonia, food refusal, severe suicidality
Admission for safety, monitoring, and treatment initiation
Continue combination therapy at least 6 months after remission
explanation.pearls: The STOP-PD II trial showed 12-month continuation of the antipsychotic (olanzapine) plus antidepressant (sertraline) after remission reduced relapse from 55 to 20 percent; the trade-off is metabolic weight gain that warrants baseline and 3-monthly monitoring.

subtopic_detail: Switching to diazepam equivalent for stepwise reduction
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 46-year-old woman who has been taking oxazepam 15 mg three times daily for 4 years for generalised anxiety, initially prescribed by a previous doctor. She wants to reduce and stop and has read about withdrawal risks. She has no history of substance use. She works as an accountant and manages her business commitments. She has no current suicidal ideation and her mood is generally good. She has already commenced cognitive behavioural therapy sessions for anxiety.

Her BMI, blood pressure and screening bloods are within normal limits.

data_table.Medication history: oxazepam 15 mg TDS for 4 years, no other psychotropics
data_table.Comorbidity: no substance use, mood generally euthymic, function preserved
data_table.Support: engaged in CBT with clinical psychologist, husband supportive
data_table.Bloods: LFTs, UEC, TFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological approach?

options.text: Continue oxazepam TDS and reduce the dose by 15 mg every fortnight over 6 weeks in a monitored stepwise approach
options.rationale: Oxazepam has a short half-life (5-15 h) which causes interdose withdrawal peaks; switching to diazepam equivalent smooths withdrawal and is standard AU RACGP practice. (Source: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines

options.text: Add pregabalin 75 mg twice daily indefinitely to cover withdrawal symptoms without a taper of the benzodiazepine
options.rationale: Pregabalin has its own dependence and withdrawal profile in AU practice and is not a substitute for a structured benzodiazepine taper; some adjunctive use exists but not without tapering. (Source: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines

options.text: Ceasing oxazepam abruptly and providing propranolol 40 mg twice daily for autonomic symptoms of withdrawal
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after prolonged use risks seizures, delirium, and severe withdrawal; stepwise taper is standard and safer. (Source: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines

options.text: Switch to alprazolam 0.5 mg three times daily and taper over 6 to 8 weeks with monthly medical review appointments
options.rationale: Alprazolam is short-acting, higher potency, and greater dependence and withdrawal liability; switching from oxazepam to alprazolam increases risk rather than reduces it. (Source: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines

options.text: Switch to diazepam 15 mg daily equivalent and reduce by 10 percent of the daily dose every 2 to 4 weeks
options.rationale: Convert to a long-acting benzodiazepine (diazepam) using standard equivalence (oxazepam 15 mg approximately 5 mg diazepam; total 45 mg oxazepam approximately 15 mg diazepam), then reduce by 10 percent of daily dose every 2-4 weeks; slower near the end; guided by symptom tolerability. (Source: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines

explanation.summary: Long-term benzodiazepine deprescribing is safest when the patient is stabilised on a long-acting equivalent (diazepam preferred), then tapered by around 10 percent of the total daily dose every 2 to 4 weeks, slowing near the end. Concurrent CBT for anxiety reduces relapse. Approximate equivalents: diazepam 5 mg is equivalent to alprazolam 0.5 mg, clonazepam 0.5 mg, lorazepam 1 mg, oxazepam 15 mg, temazepam 10 mg, nitrazepam 5 mg. Abrupt cessation risks seizures and delirium in high-dose or long-duration users.
key_points: Switch to diazepam equivalent for smoother taper
Reduce by 10 percent of daily dose every 2-4 weeks
Slower reduction near the end (last third)
Concurrent CBT reduces relapse to benzodiazepine use
explanation.pearls: Withdrawal symptoms peak day 3-5 for short-acting and day 5-10 for long-acting agents; symptoms include anxiety rebound, insomnia, tremor, sweating, and rarely seizures; protracted withdrawal syndrome with perceptual disturbance can last weeks to months.

sources.label: RACGP Guidelines for the Use of Benzodiazepines

subtopic_detail: First-line agent selection when antidepressants have destabilised
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder in the crisis assessment team clinic. She was diagnosed 4 years ago after a manic episode and stabilised on lithium. Three months ago her general practitioner added sertraline for a low mood episode. Today she presents with 2 weeks of low mood, tearfulness, and hopelessness combined with pressured speech, marked irritability, racing thoughts, and reduced sleep. Suicide ideation is present without plan. She has full insight and no psychosis. Lithium level 2 days ago was 0.8 mmol/L.

Her partner has driven her to the review after concerns her mood swings have escalated.

data_table.MSE: labile affect, tearful with pressured speech, thought racing, no psychosis, insight preserved, suicidal ideation without plan
data_table.Bloods: lithium 0.8 mmol/L (0.6-1.0), TSH within normal limits, creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR >90
data_table.Medications: lithium carbonate 800 mg nocte, sertraline 100 mg mane (started 3 months ago)
data_table.Sleep: reduced from 8 to 4 hours per night in last 10 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her medication regimen?

options.text: Cease sertraline and add quetiapine 300 mg nocte for the mixed features, continuing lithium at the current dose regimen
options.rationale: Antidepressants (especially SSRIs) can precipitate mixed features or rapid cycling in bipolar; ceasing sertraline and adding an evidence-based agent for bipolar depression with mixed features (quetiapine, or add lurasidone or olanzapine plus fluoxetine) alongside ongoing lithium is standard practice. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Increase lithium to 1000 mg nocte to target a level above 0.8 mmol/L for enhanced mixed features stabilisation
options.rationale: The immediate issue is antidepressant-driven mixed features destabilisation; increasing lithium alone without stopping the SSRI does not address the driver and delays remission. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Switch sertraline to venlafaxine XR 150 mg daily to improve the depressive symptoms with more potent SNRI activity
options.rationale: Serotonin-noradrenergic antidepressants carry higher switching risk in bipolar and are not appropriate when the presentation is antidepressant-driven mixed features. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Add lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated to 100 mg over 6 weeks with continuation of both lithium and current sertraline
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is useful for bipolar depression maintenance but not for acute mixed features and does not address the destabilising antidepressant; the slow titration also delays therapeutic effect. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Continue sertraline and add diazepam 5 mg twice daily as short term symptomatic management for the current agitation
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are adjunctive symptom control at best; the driver is antidepressant-induced destabilisation and continuing sertraline perpetuates the mixed episode. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Mixed features in bipolar disorder combine depressive and manic or hypomanic symptoms and carry heightened suicide risk. Antidepressants are commonly implicated as destabilisers and should be ceased when mixed features emerge. Evidence supports atypical antipsychotics (quetiapine, olanzapine plus fluoxetine combination for depressive polarity, lurasidone) and mood stabilisers (lithium, valproate) as first-line. Lamotrigine is preventive for depressive relapse but not first-line for acute mixed features. Involve family in safety planning.
key_points: Antidepressants can precipitate mixed features; cease when this occurs
Quetiapine, lurasidone, olanzapine-fluoxetine for bipolar depression
Continue lithium at therapeutic level (0.6-1.0)
Mixed features carry higher suicide risk than pure depressive or manic
explanation.pearls: The BALANCE trial found lithium plus valproate combination superior to valproate monotherapy for relapse prevention in bipolar; olanzapine plus fluoxetine (Symbyax) has FDA approval for bipolar depression but weight gain and metabolic risk warrant baseline and 3-monthly monitoring.

subtopic_detail: Trauma-focused therapy timing versus early pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old woman 4 months after a serious motor vehicle collision in which she was the driver and a friend passenger died. She describes nightmares 4 to 5 nights per week, avoiding driving past the site, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, and intrusive memories. Sleep is 4 hours per night. Her mood is low but she has no suicidal ideation. She is functioning at reduced capacity in her work as a teacher. She has no prior mental health history and is not on any medications.

She asks what is likely to help her recover.

data_table.MSE: anxious, tearful describing the collision, no psychosis, sleep 4 hours, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Substance use: no alcohol, no illicit substances, no benzodiazepine use
data_table.Comorbidity: no diagnosed depression or anxiety, no prior trauma disclosed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg twice daily for anxiety and insomnia with plan to review at monthly intervals for symptom improvement
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes and interfere with fear-extinction learning underpinning trauma-focused therapy; they are contraindicated as PTSD treatment. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily first-line with review at 4 weeks and titration up to 200 mg for full antidepressant effect
options.rationale: SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) are second-line for PTSD when trauma-focused therapy is unavailable or refused, or when comorbid depression drives; TF therapy has larger effect sizes. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing over 8 to 12 sessions
options.rationale: Trauma-focused psychological therapy (TF-CBT or EMDR) is first-line in adult PTSD per Phoenix Australia and NICE; pharmacotherapy is added if TF therapy is refused or unavailable, or if severe comorbid depression complicates. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Prazosin 1 mg nocte titrated to 6 mg for nightmares with no other psychological or pharmacological therapy started
options.rationale: Prazosin has role for PTSD-associated nightmares but is adjunctive; first-line for the overall disorder is trauma-focused psychological therapy. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Debriefing single session with a trauma counsellor within the next week to prevent chronic PTSD development in future
options.rationale: Single-session psychological debriefing after trauma is not recommended and can worsen outcomes; established PTSD needs structured trauma-focused therapy over 8-12 sessions. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Established PTSD (symptoms persisting more than a month with functional impairment) is best treated with trauma-focused psychological therapy: TF-CBT with prolonged exposure or cognitive processing, or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR). Around 8-12 sessions are typical. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or SNRI (venlafaxine) are second-line, particularly for comorbid depression or when TF therapy is refused or unavailable. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated because they impair fear-extinction learning. Prazosin is adjunctive for PTSD-associated nightmares. Single-session debriefing after trauma has no benefit and may harm.
key_points: First-line PTSD: TF-CBT or EMDR, 8-12 sessions
SSRI/SNRI second-line or adjunct for depression/anxiety
Benzodiazepines contraindicated in PTSD
Prazosin adjunct for nightmares
explanation.pearls: Prolonged exposure therapy uses in-vivo and imaginal exposure to trauma cues to habituate the fear response; cognitive processing therapy targets stuck-point beliefs; both have around 60-70 percent response rate with sustained benefit at 12 months.

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic selection when cannabis co-morbidity is dominant
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in the early psychosis service reviewing a 20-year-old university student with 3 weeks of increasingly disorganised speech, persecutory delusions that his housemates are recording him, and third-person auditory hallucinations. He has been smoking around 3 g of high-potency cannabis daily for 18 months, with insight lost 4 weeks ago. He is otherwise physically well. There is a paternal uncle with schizophrenia. He has no prior psychiatric contact. He is currently residing with his mother who has agreed to support him at home during any pharmacotherapy trial.

He accepts oral treatment and refuses depot injection at this stage.

data_table.MSE: disorganised speech, persecutory delusions, third-person AH, no suicidal ideation, insight impaired
data_table.Bloods: urea, electrolytes, LFTs, TSH, glucose, lipids, prolactin within normal limits
data_table.Urine drug screen: positive THC, negative amphetamines, cocaine, opioids
data_table.Weight: 78 kg, BMI 24, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HDL 1.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oral antipsychotic choice?

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg nocte titrated to 20 mg as first-line therapy given its rapid effect and reliable response
options.rationale: Olanzapine has substantial metabolic burden (weight gain 5-12 kg in first year) and is not recommended first-line in first episode psychosis per RANZCP; risperidone or aripiprazole are preferred for their metabolic profile and dopaminergic effect. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Chlorpromazine 100 mg three times daily as a broad spectrum first line agent with mild sedative benefit for sleep
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics carry high EPS risk and are not first-line in first episode psychosis; second-generation agents (risperidone or aripiprazole) are standard. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Clozapine 12.5 mg twice daily titrated to 300 mg to address treatment-resistant cannabis-related psychosis quickly
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of 2 antipsychotics at adequate dose and duration); it is not first-line in first episode psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Risperidone 1 mg twice daily titrated to 2 to 4 mg over 1 week with monitoring for extrapyramidal side effects
options.rationale: Risperidone or aripiprazole are first-line in first episode psychosis per RANZCP CPG because of the more favourable metabolic profile; low starting dose with weekly titration to 2-4 mg is standard, with EPS monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Quetiapine 300 mg nocte titrated to 600 mg as first line agent to improve sleep and reduce paranoid ideation
options.rationale: Quetiapine is used but has weaker antipsychotic effect at low doses and is often subtherapeutic; risperidone or aripiprazole are preferred first-line per RANZCP with better response in first episode psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

explanation.summary: First episode psychosis carries a favourable response rate to low-dose second-generation antipsychotics; RANZCP recommends risperidone or aripiprazole first-line because of the metabolic profile relative to olanzapine and clozapine. Start low and titrate slowly (risperidone 1 mg BD to 2-4 mg total; aripiprazole 10 mg to 15 mg daily) with monitoring for EPS. Substance use co-management (cannabis in particular) is essential as continued use predicts poorer response and relapse. Family psychoeducation and vocational support are cornerstones. Metabolic baseline and 3-monthly monitoring (weight, waist, glucose, lipids, BP) is required.
key_points: Risperidone or aripiprazole first-line in first episode
Low starting dose, slow titration, EPS monitoring
Cannabis co-management essential
Metabolic baseline and 3-monthly monitoring
explanation.pearls: Around 60-80 percent of first episode psychosis responds within 6 weeks to adequate dose; treatment for at least 12 to 24 months after remission is standard, with individualised discussion around continuation, given up to 80 percent relapse rate if stopped after single episode remission.

subtopic_detail: SSRI selection when breastfeeding an exclusively breastfed newborn
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatrist reviewing a 32-year-old G1P1 who is 6 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding a term male infant. She reports 4 weeks of pervasive low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia, guilt about not enjoying her baby, and early morning waking. EPDS score today is 18. She has passive suicidal ideation without plan and no thoughts of harming her baby. She has good social support with her partner and her mother visiting daily. Sleep is fragmented but the baby is feeding and gaining weight well. She has no personal history of depression prior to this pregnancy.

She would prefer to continue breastfeeding if safe to do so and asks about medication options today.

data_table.MSE: flat affect, tearful, thought content of guilt and hopelessness, no psychosis, passive SI no plan, insight intact
data_table.Infant: 6-week-old term male, exclusively breastfed, gaining weight along 50th centile
data_table.Bloods: TSH, iron studies, ferritin, B12 within normal limits, no anaemia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line SSRI to prescribe?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily as the first line SSRI in breastfeeding with review at 2 weeks for response and tolerability
options.rationale: Sertraline has the strongest safety data in breastfeeding, with negligible infant serum levels and low relative infant dose (<2 percent); it is first-line SSRI in perinatal depression per Beyond Blue and LactMed. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily as first line agent, with reduction to alternate day dosing if the infant develops symptoms
options.rationale: Fluoxetine and its active metabolite norfluoxetine have long half-lives (2-4 days and 7-15 days respectively), leading to higher infant serum levels compared to sertraline; sertraline or paroxetine are preferred in breastfeeding. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

options.text: Escitalopram 10 mg daily as it has a favourable side effect profile and gentle onset for postnatal use in mothers
options.rationale: Escitalopram is second-line in breastfeeding; sertraline has more robust safety data and lower relative infant dose in the perinatal literature. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

options.text: Venlafaxine XR 75 mg daily as an SNRI to address concurrent anxiety symptoms with the depressed mood presenting
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has less breastfeeding safety data than sertraline and is not first-line perinatally; SSRIs (sertraline preferred) are first-line for depression with mixed anxiety features in breastfeeding mothers. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

options.text: St John's wort standardised extract 300 mg three times daily as a natural alternative for mild to moderate depression
options.rationale: St John's wort is not recommended in breastfeeding due to inconsistent standardisation, drug interactions (CYP3A4 inducer), and infant safety uncertainty; sertraline is first-line. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

explanation.summary: Postnatal depression affects around 10-15 percent of new mothers and warrants active treatment given impact on infant attachment, cognitive and emotional development. Sertraline has the strongest breastfeeding safety data of the SSRIs, with negligible infant serum levels and no reported adverse effects at therapeutic maternal doses. Start 50 mg daily (25 mg for the first 3 days if anxious features) and review at 2 weeks. Psychological therapy (interpersonal therapy or CBT) is offered concurrently. Postpartum psychosis or severe depression with active suicidal or infanticidal ideation warrants urgent psychiatric admission with mother-baby unit consideration.
key_points: Sertraline first-line SSRI in breastfeeding (low RID)
Paroxetine also acceptable in breastfeeding
Fluoxetine higher infant serum levels (long half-life)
IPT or CBT concurrent psychological therapy
explanation.pearls: The relative infant dose (RID) for sertraline is around 0.5-2 percent of maternal weight-adjusted dose; the general threshold of concern is 10 percent; monitor infant for sedation, feeding, weight gain, and irritability.

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic clarification when cognitive complaints coexist
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 74-year-old retired teacher accompanied by his wife with 6 months of progressive loss of interest, low energy, appetite loss with 5 kg weight loss, and complaints of poor memory and concentration. His wife reports he says he is a burden. He denies suicidal plans. On testing he scores poorly on serial 7s citing lack of effort, but recall is intact with cueing. His Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination is 82 out of 100 with a global reduction (not domain-specific). CT brain 6 months ago was unremarkable for atrophy or vascular changes.

He has hypertension controlled with perindopril and no other medications.

data_table.MSE: flat affect, psychomotor slowing, thought content of guilt and worthlessness, no psychosis, passive suicidal ideation no plan
data_table.Cognitive: ACE 82/100 with global reduction, recall improves with semantic cueing, no focal deficits
data_table.Bloods: TSH, B12, folate, calcium, urea, electrolytes, LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Refer for donepezil trial as a therapeutic diagnostic step for early Alzheimer's disease with treatment response
options.rationale: Cognitive picture with intact recall on cueing, global (not domain-specific) reduction, and depressive symptoms fits pseudodementia rather than Alzheimer's; treating depression first clarifies the diagnosis and avoids inappropriate cholinesterase inhibitor exposure. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Refer for immediate lumbar puncture and CSF amyloid biomarkers before any medication trial to establish diagnosis clearly
options.rationale: CSF biomarkers are not first-line in this scenario where depression is a strong alternative explanation; treat depression first, then reassess cognition and consider structural imaging or biomarker referral if deficits persist. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg daily titrated to 50 mg with cognitive reassessment at 8 to 12 weeks after remission achieved
options.rationale: Depressive pseudodementia is common in late-life depression; recall improving with cueing, global cognitive reduction, and prominent depressive features support depression as primary; treat with an SSRI at reduced starting dose (elderly), then reassess cognition 8-12 weeks after mood remission. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Order MRI brain with hippocampal volumes prior to any treatment intervention to define underlying neurodegeneration presence
options.rationale: MRI is useful when structural cause is suspected but should not delay treatment of clearly identified depression; treat first and image if cognitive deficits persist after mood remission. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Start memantine 5 mg daily titrated to 20 mg for suspected moderate Alzheimer's disease as a therapeutic diagnostic step
options.rationale: Memantine is for moderate to severe Alzheimer's, not a diagnostic trial; and the clinical picture supports pseudodementia rather than established dementia at this point. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Depressive pseudodementia is late-life depression presenting with prominent cognitive complaints. Distinguishing features from Alzheimer's disease include prominent affective symptoms, insight into cognitive change (complaining rather than concealing), global rather than domain-specific cognitive reduction, recall improving with cueing, poor effort on testing, and preserved autobiographical memory. Treat depression with an SSRI at reduced starting dose (elderly) and reassess cognition 8-12 weeks after mood remission. Persistent cognitive deficits after mood remission warrant further neurodegenerative workup including MRI and neuropsychology.
key_points: Pseudodementia: prominent depression, insight preserved
Recall improves with cueing (not seen in Alzheimer's)
SSRI first-line, reduced starting dose in elderly
Reassess cognition 8-12 weeks after mood remission
explanation.pearls: Up to 40 percent of pseudodementia patients develop true dementia within 5 years; ongoing cognitive monitoring is warranted even after mood remission; consider MRI, neuropsychology, and possible CSF biomarkers if cognition does not fully recover.

subtopic_detail: Escalation pathway when non-pharmacological measures have failed
stem:
You are the child and adolescent psychiatry registrar reviewing a 15-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder (level 3, minimally verbal) and moderate intellectual disability. His mother reports 3 months of escalating head-banging producing scalp abrasions, biting his hand producing skin breaks, and hitting his siblings when transitions occur. A structured behavioural plan with visual schedules, sensory environment modification, and functional communication training has been implemented by his ABA team for 3 months with limited response. Sleep is 4 hours per night. Medical review has excluded pain (dental, constipation, otitis).

He has never been on psychotropic medication.

data_table.Diagnostic: ASD level 3, minimally verbal, moderate ID (WISC-V IQ 45)
data_table.Behaviour: SIB (head banging, self biting) plus aggression at transitions
data_table.Medical workup: no dental caries, no otitis media, no constipation, urinalysis clear
data_table.Non-pharmacological: 3 months structured ABA and visual schedule with limited response

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Melatonin 3 mg nocte only, targeting sleep with the hope this reduces daytime irritability and self injurious behaviour
options.rationale: Melatonin may help sleep initiation but does not treat established self-injurious behaviour or aggression; when behavioural measures have failed and injury risk is present, targeted pharmacotherapy is indicated. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

options.text: Clonidine 25 micrograms nocte for arousal reduction and hyperactivity as an alternative to antipsychotic exposure
options.rationale: Clonidine is used for ADHD-symptom overlap and sleep in autism but has weaker evidence than risperidone or aripiprazole for irritability and self injurious behaviour of the severity described. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg twice daily as first line to reduce agitation and self injurious behaviour at difficult transition periods
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines cause paradoxical disinhibition in autism and intellectual disability and are not first-line; risperidone or aripiprazole is preferred with better evidence. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

options.text: Fluoxetine 10 mg daily as first line for rigid repetitive behaviours with plan to add antipsychotic only if it fails
options.rationale: SSRIs have limited evidence for irritability and aggression in autism and may worsen agitation, particularly in intellectual disability; risperidone or aripiprazole is preferred for irritability with SIB. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

options.text: Risperidone 0.25 mg nocte, titrating slowly to 0.5 mg BD, with metabolic monitoring baseline and every 3 months planned
options.rationale: Risperidone (or aripiprazole) is TGA-indicated for irritability and aggression in autism when behavioural interventions have failed; slow titration and metabolic baseline plus 3-monthly monitoring are required to minimise weight gain, hyperprolactinaemia, and metabolic burden. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

explanation.summary: Escalating self-injurious behaviour and aggression in an autistic adolescent with intellectual disability warrants a structured medical (rule out pain, constipation, dental, otitis) and behavioural (functional analysis, visual schedules, sensory adaptations) assessment first. When these are optimised and injury risk remains, risperidone or aripiprazole are the two agents with the strongest evidence and TGA indication in Australia for irritability associated with autism. Titrate slowly from a low starting dose (risperidone 0.25 mg nocte) with metabolic baseline (weight, waist, glucose, lipids, prolactin, BP) and monitoring every 3 months. Reassess indication regularly and taper when clinically stable.
key_points: Rule out pain, constipation, dental, otitis before pharmacotherapy
Risperidone or aripiprazole first-line for autism irritability
Metabolic baseline and 3-monthly monitoring
Reassess indication and taper when stable
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole tends to cause less weight gain and hyperprolactinaemia than risperidone but higher akathisia; both have TGA approval for autism-associated irritability; typical response emerges within 2-4 weeks.

subtopic_detail: IV sodium bicarbonate threshold for QRS widening
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 25-year-old woman brought in by her flatmate 90 minutes after finding empty amitriptyline packets and a suicide note. She had been prescribed amitriptyline 25 mg tablets for chronic migraine. She estimates 40 tablets ingested. She is drowsy but rousable and has vomited once en route.

Her flatmate confirms she has been increasingly withdrawn over recent weeks after relationship breakdown and university stress.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.ECG: sinus tachycardia rate 128, QRS 132 ms (upper limit 100 ms), terminal R wave in aVR 5 mm, no arrhythmia
data_table.Venous blood gas: pH 7.28, pCO2 34 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L (<2.0), potassium 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer 100 mmol (100 mL of 8.4 percent) IV sodium bicarbonate as a rapid push and repeat targeting QRS below 100 ms and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55
options.rationale: QRS widening beyond 100 ms in TCA overdose reflects sodium channel blockade and predicts VT/VF. The intervention is IV sodium bicarbonate boluses (1-2 mmol/kg, i.e. 100 mmol here) titrated to narrow QRS below 100 ms and to alkalinise pH to 7.45-7.55. Alkalinisation shifts drug away from cardiac sodium channels via protein binding and reduces free drug. This is a class I recommendation in the AU Toxicology & Toxinology Poisons Information text. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

options.text: Administer IV flumazenil 200 micrograms in 15 second increments to reverse sedation and reassess neurological status once alert
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures in a patient at risk of pro-convulsant drug effects; TCAs lower seizure threshold and flumazenil unmasks epileptogenic drug effects. It also does not reverse TCA toxicity. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

options.text: Give IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes to prevent progression to malignant ventricular arrhythmia in the context of QRS prolongation
options.rationale: Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics (procainamide, flecainide) and class III agents that prolong QT (amiodarone, sotalol) worsen TCA cardiotoxicity by further blocking sodium channels or prolonging repolarisation. Sodium bicarbonate is the specific antidote. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

options.text: Empirical activated charcoal 50 g orally now to reduce further absorption of the ingested tablets in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is considered within one hour of ingestion in patients with intact airway; at 90 minutes with reduced GCS the risk of aspiration outweighs the benefit unless the airway is secured. Sodium bicarbonate takes priority for the cardiotoxic manifestation. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

options.text: IV hypertonic 3 percent saline 100 mL over 30 minutes to correct the sodium status and stabilise cardiac membranes
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline does not have the same sodium-channel-shifting effect as bicarbonate because it does not alkalinise, and the therapeutic effect is combined sodium load AND alkalinisation. Bicarbonate is the specific treatment. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

explanation.summary: TCA toxicity produces anticholinergic, alpha-blocking, sodium channel blocking and CNS depressant effects. Cardiovascular toxicity is the leading cause of death: QRS widening beyond 100 ms predicts seizures, above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia.
